items.title: Mali: Army, Russia’s ‘Africa Corps’ Commit New Abuses
items.description: Click to expand Image Aftermath of the apparent Malian military drone strike on September 16, 2026, in Guélédié village, Mopti region, Mali. Screenshots from video analyzed and geolocated by Human Rights Watch. © Private (Nairobi) – Mali’s armed forces and the allied Russia-controlled Africa Corps have committed new atrocities against civilians in central Mali during renewed fighting, Human Rights Watch said today. On September 16, 2026, an apparent military drone strike in Guélédié village, Mopti region, killed eight civilians and injured at least six others. Between May and August, Malian and Africa Corps forces held numerous detainees inhumanely in a metal container at an army base in Sévaré town, Mopti region, where many were tortured, including with severe beatings, electric shock, and waterboarding. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of the Mali junta’s failure to rein in its abusive forces and allies,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Recent atrocities implicate the Malian army as well as Russia-controlled Africa Corps, for which Russian officials should also be held accountable.” The Malian army’s offensive followed coordinated attacks across Mali by the Al Qaeda-linked Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, JNIM) and the Azawad Liberation Front (Front de Libération de l’Azawad, FLA) in late April. Malian forces and the allied Africa Corps killed civilians, including many children, and destroyed civilian property and health facilities in airstrikes and other attacks. Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed fifteen people between August and September, including three witnesses in Guélédié, four former detainees at the Sévaré military base, and eight members of nongovernmental organizations. Human Rights Watch sent letters to the Malian and Russian defense ministers in early October but received no responses. Guélédié On September 16 at about 10 a.m., an apparent military drone delivered a munition on civilians on the outskirts of Guélédié village, killing eight men, ages 25 to 40, and injuring six others. The villagers had gathered around a tree, where a man was providing paid internet access via Starlink. Residents said JNIM fighters often used this service to support operations. Witnesses said a drone flew over the village for about one hour before delivering its munition, suggesting that the area was being surveilled. “The drone passed over the village at about 9 a.m. and came back at least four times,” said a 40-year-old man. “It was white and had long, thin, straight wings. It would spin around, disappear, and come back again.” This description is broadly consistent with larger drones the Malian government is known to use. Witnesses said that JNIM has a base in Guélédié and over 100 JNIM fighters were present in the village at the time of the strike, although no JNIM fighters were among the casualties. They also said JNIM fighters alerted the local population via WhatsApp about the possibility of a drone strike at the Starlink location, before leaving the area along with many civilians. Witnesses said that only 14 civilians had remained at the site, continuing to use the connection, when the drone delivered its munition. “The explosion was deafening, really strong,” said a 30-year-old villager. “I saw very thick black smoke rising from the Starlink connection area.” A 52-year-old health worker said he went to the scene about an hour later and found six men dead and seven injured “with their bodies burned,” one of whom died there. He said he called the Ténenkou military base commander and that he would take the injured to the Ténenkou Referral Health Center there. “But he did not only categorically refuse our evacuating them,” the health worker said. “But he also warned me not to provide them with any support. For him, they were JNIM fighters and he told me that the drone could not have targeted civilians.” The injured were eventually evacuated. In a September 24 statement, Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières, MSF) said its staff at the health center treated four “seriously injured” people with “burns over their entire bodies,” and one “died shortly after arrival.” Human Rights Watch verified a video shared by witnesses of the aftermath of the strike and geolocated it to an area about 600 meters northeast of the village center. It shows the bodies of three men, two under a burned and broken tree and one in a nearby pond. Two burned motorcycles and a destroyed solar panel are also visible. In a September 17 statement, the armed forces chief of staff said that on September 16, military units “spotted terrorist elements concealed under vegetation northeast of Guélédié” with “war equipment and satellite communication devices,” after which they “neutralized” them and destroyed their equipment. Mali’s junta has increasingly used airstrikes against armed groups. Human Rights Watch, other human rights groups, and severalmedia and investigative organizations have documented airstrikes that killed civilians. Sévaré The Malian military and the Africa Corps have taken hundreds of civilians into custody during counterinsurgency operations across Mali and unlawfully detained many in military bases. Human Rights Watch, other human rights groups, and the media have documented torture at several bases. On May 7, soldiers and Africa Corps fighters apprehended a 30-year-old civilian at his home in Guirowel, a village in a JNIM-controlled area in Mopti region. On July 4, they arrested three Quranic students, ages 32, 37, and 40, in Thy village, Mopti region, following a JNIM attack on a military position there. The four men later said the forces took them to the Hamadoun Bocary Barry army base in Sévaré, holding them incommunicado in a shipping container about 20 meters long with no windows, toilet, or washing facilities, in extreme heat without ventilation, alongside dozens of other detainees. The men said they received a small amount of poor-quality food once a day, were denied necessary medical care, and were verbally abused. “We got a small piece of bread and sometimes beans and half a bottle of water once a day,” said the 32-year-old man. “The heat was unbearable. On the first day, we were 27, but over the days we reached more than 70 people. We relieved ourselves in a bucket, it was always full and spilling onto the floor. They didn’t empty it.” The men said they identified Malian soldiers by their uniforms and languages, including French, Bambara, and Fulfulde. They said Africa Corps fighters had “light skin” and spoke a foreign language they did not understand. Three of the men said Malian soldiers and Africa Corps fighters repeatedly tortured them in a room in a building near the base entrance, alongside Sévaré’s main road, so they could hear traffic sounds. The room had a metal bed, a barrel filled with water, a table, and electric wires on the floor, where the men said they were tortured and interrogated to confess to their alleged association with JNIM. The man from Guirowel said Malian and Africa Corps personnel tortured him twice for about two hours each. “I almost lost my life when two Russian soldiers drowned me in a barrel of water,” he said. “Every time I lost consciousness, I was resuscitated with an electric shock and drowned again. “They burned my buttocks with hot plastic, and they lit a cloth on my back. They forced me to give information about JNIM, and to admit I was a fighter.” The 37-year-old man said a Malian soldier tied him to a bed and demanded: “Tell us everything or we’ll kill you.” Then “the blows started raining down on my buttocks and back. ‘Talk!’ they said to me. [A] soldier choked my neck and banged my head against the bed. I don't remember anything after that.” The 40-year-old man said soldiers tied his feet to a bed and threatened to kill him if he withheld information about JNIM fighters. “I was hit on my buttocks, fire [put] on my back,” he said. “A soldier held my penis and put electricity on it,” while another “poured water on my back and hit me.” The men said several detainees died in the container following torture. “When a prisoner was about to die, we would bang on the door to alert the guards,” said the 40-year-old man. “They told us to inform them only when a person died. They had no mercy. Eight people died during my detention.” The military released the three men from Thy on July 20 and the man from Guirowel on August 6. Relatives reportedly paid the military 1.8 million CFA francs (about US$3,000) for the three Thy men and 1 million CFA (about $1,800) for the Guirowel man to secure their release. All parties to Mali’s armed conflict are bound by international humanitarian law, notably Common Article 3 and Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 as well as customary laws of war. Parties must take all feasible precautions before an attack, including verifying that the target is a military objective. Attacks with no military objective or that do not distinguish between civilians and military personnel are unlawfully indiscriminate. Anyone deprived of their liberty must be treated humanely in all circumstances and protected against murder, torture, and cruel, humiliating, and degrading treatment. Denying medical care to the wounded or detainees can be a war crime. Individuals who commit serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent or as a matter of command responsibility may be prosecuted for war crimes. In March, the United Nations Human Rights Council renewed the mandate of the independent expert on Mali to assess the human rights situation and assist national authorities in promoting human rights and the rule of law. “These recent abuses should serve as a stark reminder that concerned governments and international institutions should press the Malian authorities to conduct credible investigations into military abuses and bring those responsible to justice,” Allegrozzi said. “The UN Human Rights Council should increase its scrutiny of the situation in Mali and take steps to prevent further abuses."

items.title: Spurring economic growth
items.description: THE World Bank’s Reclaiming Momentum Towards Prosperity report presents a sobering reality: poverty has climbed back to 25.3 per cent on the national line; and close to 45pc of Pakistanis fall below the bank’s new $4.20-a-day threshold. Stabilising our way into deeper poverty has exposed the limits of conventional macroeconomic management. Speaking last week at the International Conference on Inclusive and Resilient Economic Empowerment and Growth, organised by the Pakistan Poverty Alleviation Fund in Islamabad, I put one question at the centre: how do we break this cycle? Accelerating growth requires recognising where real growth originates. Pakistan’s largest capital investment of this decade never appeared in a Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP), Annual Development Programme (ADP), or Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). Farmers, shopkeepers and households imported about 17 gigawatts of solar panels in 2024, and the same again in 2025. No PC-1. No donor. No climate finance unit. They used their own savings, because diesel costs and the unwinding of unsustainable energy subsidies made it rational. The lesson for macroeconomic policy is direct. Prolonged, distorted subsidies are not a safety net. They are an obstacle to citizen-led growth. When fiscal pressure forced the state to pare them back, citizens moved faster than planners to protect their own balance sheets. The state’s response was to tax panel imports and revise net-metering terms. So when we ask how planning can accelerate growth, we should first admit that citizens are already ahead of the plan. The question is whether the state will remove the friction in their way or keep chasing donors. Three shifts would make the difference. Unpriced risk: Macroeconomic stability cannot survive risk that no one has priced. Pakistan already has a climate budget. It is not the one captured by the recently introduced climate budget tagging. It is the one written after each disaster. Major floods now produce post-disaster needs assessments, reconstruction budgets, and emergency appeals. That is our real climate expenditure: unplanned and largely borrowed — a permanent drag on fiscal space. The fix is not more tagging of development spending. It is pricing climate risk before it arrives. Pakistan already has a climate budget — the one written after each disaster. In practice, this means treating climate losses as a contingent liability of each province, the way we already treat circular debt and SOE guarantees. The Fiscal Risk Statement mentions disasters but puts no number on them. Each province can estimate its average annual loss from floods, heat, and drought, and appropriate a share of it every year as an expected cost. Budget theorists call this ‘expected-value budgeting’. A loss that is budgeted becomes a decision. A loss that is not budgeted becomes a bailout, often paid through the Benazir Income Support Programme’s emergency transfers. Maintenance first: Economic productivity depends on assets that work. That makes resilience a maintenance problem before it is a development problem. Embankments, drains, canals, and roads do not fail because nobody built them. They fail because their recurrent budgets are starved. Yet our economic conversation stays inside the development budget. The federal PSDP alone carries a throw-forward of about Rs11 trillion, and new schemes keep joining the queue, while existing assets go unmaintained. The ADP builds the embankment. The operations and maintenance line decides whether it holds. Protecting maintenance allocations for water assets would preserve existing capital and buy more resilience per rupee than most new projects. One can see where local money is actually spent. The most local spending stream is not an SDG-linked programme. It is the parliamentarians’ development schemes: tube-wells, link roads, drains, and culverts. They are quick, uncoordinated, and climate-blind. Nobody screens them. A single check asking whether the asset will survive the next monsoon would protect more local capital than every formal climate project combined. Green growth at the local level will not come from specialised projects. It will come when ordinary public spending stops creating new fiscal liabilities. District arithmetic: Growth targets fail when they stay abstract. The NDC is written in tonnes of carbon and gigawatts. A district plans in culverts, acres, and tube-wells. Nobody has done the translation. A union council cannot own or deliver a national target expressed in metrics it does not know. The first mechanism is a translation layer. Each district needs a short climate investment and growth plan that converts national targets into local units: acres under laser levelling and drip irrigation, tube-wells solarised, kilometres of drains cleared. Once a target is counted in local units, a local official can be held accountable for it. The second mechanism is money that rewards performance instead of rescuing failure. Versions of this model already work elsewhere. A district that sets up its own climate fund and meets basic public financial management standards qualifies for performance-based grants spent on investments its communities choose. Money follows institutions, not proposals. Pakistan could pilot this in 10 of its most flood-exposed districts through provincial finance commission transfers, with the grant rising as each district meets its conditions. That is local ownership with a test attached. The third mechanism is creditworthiness. Local growth stays dependent on donor projects because no district or municipal body can borrow or issue a municipal bond. None has a balance sheet, an asset inventory, audited accounts, or a credit rating. A provincial pooled financing facility could bundle bankable projects, such as solar for water supply, municipal waste, and cold storage, and raise capital against the pool. The precondition is unglamorous: audited accounts and own-source revenue at local level. Investors do not lend to plans. They lend to entities with a record. The fourth point is simpler. For most local investment, the bottleneck is not finance. It is permission. A solar mini-grid needs a Disco connection and a Nepra licence. A restoration project needs a land lease. A water scheme needs water rights. Locally owned investment needs a single district window for permissions before it needs another fund. In all: price the loss before the flood. Fund maintenance before new projects. Count targets in district units. Make municipalities bankable. Citizens have already shown, panel by panel, even when they are below the poverty line, that they will finance their own resilience. The state cannot lead them, but can stop taxing their initiative and carry the risks they cannot. The writer is a climate expert. Published in Dawn, October 22nd, 2026

items.title: Makkah pact clarity
items.description: THERE had been much speculation about what exactly the trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement entails, other than general commitments about the collective defence of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye. But with the release of the text of the 16-article agreement, there is now some clarity about its objectives. While Article 2 says that an “externally originating armed attack” on any of the signatories will be considered an attack on all, triggering the right of self-defence under the UN Charter, the agreement is silent on offensive action. This should settle questions about the extent of involvement of the pact allies in the ongoing Saudi-Houthi war, and any future engagement. That it is a purely defensive arrangement was also echoed by the Turkish foreign minister. He stressed it was not an “offensive agreement”, and ruled out sending his country’s troops to a foreign theatre. Other salient features of the pact include joint defence production, intelligence sharing and the interoperability of forces. Such clarity is welcome. While the defence of Saudi Arabia is important, Pakistan, Turkiye, and other regional states should continue efforts to find a negotiated solution to the Yemen conflict — both between the Saudis and Houthis and within Yemen. In a related development, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces was in Tehran on Tuesday to try and prevent further escalation on the war front. The message from Tehran is that the US should accept Iran’s seven-point proposal if talks are to restart. A key Iranian demand is a ceasefire on all fronts, the end of the American blockade, lifting of sanctions, and the release of the Islamic Republic’s funds. However, despite the efforts of Pakistan and others, there are troubling noises coming from Washington and Tel Aviv. The abrasive US war secretary — who is no proponent of peace and dialogue — was recently in Israel , while the Israeli prime minister, who will be fighting for his political survival in next week’s elections, has said he and President Donald Trump need to ‘eliminate’ the “Iranian regime”. Even the sincerest effort to bring peace to the Gulf, Yemen, and the wider Middle East will come to naught if the US and Israel continue with their provocative behaviour. A strike on Iran after the Israeli and US elections would be a massive blunder, and if there are any mature advisers left in Washington, they should talk the US president out of making any such move, besides warning Tel Aviv against such arrogant action. Iran may be under pressure, but as the past several months have shown, it has the capacity to withstand considerable pain inflicted on it by the US and Israel. Fresh aggression can kick off a firestorm that will be in no one’s control, hence it is best to abandon such reckless plans. Published in Dawn, October 22nd, 2026

items.title: Buscador | Madrid copa los barrios más caros para comprar o alquilar casa en las grandes ciudades
items.description: Vivir de alquiler supone un esfuerzo mayúsculo para muchos bolsillos, y puede llegar a resultar asfixiante para las finanzas de numerosos hogares en varias ciudades del país. En algunos barrios de Madrid, de hecho, se ha convertido casi en una quimera . Según los últimos datos del Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), publicados este miércoles, 36 de los 50 barrios más caros de España para ser inquilino se concentran en la capital. El más costoso de todos es Recoletos, donde el arrendamiento mensual medio alcanza los 2.037 euros. Le siguen Pedralbes, en Barcelona, y Piovera, de nuevo en Madrid, ambos con una renta media de 2.002 euros. En total, doce barrios barceloneses aparecen en esta clasificación, que completan Malagueta-Limonar, en Málaga (1.214 euros), y El Pla de Remei-Gran Via, en Valencia (1.167). Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Cuántas casas más puede construir España?
items.description: A España le faltan ya unas 750.000 viviendas para cubrir la demanda existente, según los cálculos del Banco de España. Y la brecha sigue creciendo: si se mantienen los actuales flujos migratorios y el ritmo de creación de hogares (más de 200.000 al año), el déficit podría alcanzar el millón de viviendas en 2030. Cubrir ese agujero recae en buena medida sobre el sector de la construcción y promoción, que pide agilizar trámites burocráticos y liberar más suelo, aunque duda sobre la capacidad de sus empresas para crecer. Problemas de financiación y escasez de mano de obra se interponen en esa misión. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Maldives president, CDF Munir stress importance of strengthening defence cooperation
items.description: Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and visiting Maldivian President Dr Mohamed Muizzu underscored the importance of strengthening bilateral defence cooperation on Wednesday, state-run Radio Pakistan reported . Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established in 1966. CDF Munir called on the visiting president in Islamabad, where the two leaders discussed matters of mutual interest, the prevailing regional security environment, and avenues for enhancing bilateral cooperation, the Radio Pakistan report said. “Both sides underscored the importance of strengthening defence cooperation, institutional linkages and professional exchanges,” it added. The CDF highlighted the “longstanding and cordial relations” between the two countries. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening bilateral cooperation and promoting peace, stability and security in the region through constructive engagement, Radio Pakistan said. It added that President Muizzu commended the professionalism of Pakistan’s armed forces and appreciated the country’s continued efforts to promote regional peace and stability. PM Shehbaz vows strengthening of bilateral relations Earlier, PM Shehbaz vowed to strengthen bilateral relations with the Maldives, as the two countries signed 20 memorandums of understanding (MoUs). Addressing a joint press stakeout following the signing of 20 wide-ranging MoUs, PM Shehbaz said, “There is no doubt that the two countries [will] keep on strengthening these relations for all time to come.” The premier extended a “very warm welcome” to the visiting dignitary and his delegation. PM Shehbaz expressed his “warmest greetings and heartfelt affection to the people of Dhivehi Raajje, the land of islands, a nation whose spirit is as vast as the ocean that surrounds it,” hailing 60 years of diplomatic ties between the two countries. The prime minister noted that he and Muizzu, in their bilateral and delegation-level talks, discussed “all important issues which have direct bearing between our two brotherly countries and of course, regional and international issues”. “I am very happy to announce that we had a wonderful session, very productive and very fruitful discussions,” he remarked. PM Shehbaz noted that the conversations encompassed “economic and trade relations, our strategic defence cooperation, our support for training of our brothers and sisters from Maldives in Pakistan in various walks of life; police, defence, education, health and many other” fields. The prime minister went on to announce that both sides had agreed to raise their bilateral trade from $13.9 million — “just a fraction of our potential” — to $200m in the next two years. Highlighting that the two South Asian countries had “very strong” relations, coupled with a “long list of mutual achievements”, PM Shehbaz said both sides noted that their ties “do not reflect the true strength of our economic cooperation”. Thanking Muizzu for his “personal support in this behalf”, the premier went on to announce that Islamabad would support Malé in promoting the plantation of 5m trees in the Maldives by providing 100,000 olive cuttings and 100,000 seeds of various plant species within a mutually decided timeframe. Referring to the MoUs signed, he affirmed that he “will be very happy to personally work with [Muizzu] to translate these written MoUs into action with prompt decision-making and speedy implementation”. The prime minister declared that Pakistan was “absolutely ready to provide technical expertise to various segments of our mutual cooperation and, above all, Pakistan is very happy to learn that Maldives is moving forward speedily to establish data centres in other places”. “This is great news, and as a matter of good luck, Pakistan has also attained a reasonable level of expertise and professional capability in this field,” he added, noting that the country had set up data centres in various locations. He offered Pakistan’s “experience and our professional capabilities in this behalf” to the Maldives. PM Shehbaz noted that a large number of Maldivian students were receiving education in Pakistani universities and colleges, particularly in the field of healthcare, and that 250 Pakistani doctors and other paramedics were serving in the Maldives. “This shall continue in future with bigger numbers so that whatever requirements you have, we as a brotherly country would be more than happy to fulfil those requirements willingly and with utmost sincerity of purpose,” the prime minister said. Speaking on international developments, PM Shehbaz commended the Maldives’ “unwavering” support for the Palestinian cause, adding that Islamabad remains fully committed to the Palestinians’ right of self-determination and the establishment of an independent state of Palestine. The premier further said he briefed Muizzu on Pakistan’s principled position on occupied Jammu and Kashmir, declaring Islamabad’s support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. “Till they have won their struggle and gotten the right of self-determination, Pakistan shall continue to support them diplomatically and, of course, support them at all international forums till they become an independent sovereign country as per UNSC resolutions, and their sacrifice will not go to waste at all,” he said. The prime minister also expressed Pakistan’s “serious concern” over India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance in April 2025, pointing out that it was a violation of an international binding treaty. “Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponised or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he stated. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan has made it “abundantly clear at various forums ”, including the UN General Assembly last month, that water was a “red line” for the country. “Waterflows in any canal or ocean, sea or straits, carries trade, commerce, message of prosperity and progress, and not threats, confrontations and conflicts,” he said. “Water is a lifeline for humanity […] so this should be known to all and sundry that any violation in this behalf will be regarded by Pakistan as an act of war,” the prime minister warned. Concluding his remarks, PM Shehbaz said Muizzu’s visit had given Pakistan-Maldives relations “new purpose and new momentum”. He remarked, “The same ocean that touches the shores of Karachi and Gwadar embraces the islands of the Maldives. “For centuries, its waves have carried traders, scholars and travellers between our lands. Today, they carry the renewed promise of our wonderful friendship whose finest chapters are yet to be written.” In his comments, Muizzu appreciated PM Shehbaz, the government and people of Pakistan for “their exceptional warmth and gracious hospitality”. He added that his visit coming on the 60-year mark of Pakistan-Maldives diplomatic relations made it “particularly significant”. The 60 years have been marked by warmth, friendship and shared perspectives, he said. “This visit takes place after a decade-long interval. It offers us an important opportunity not simply to celebrate the friendship of the past but to define the partnership of the future,” Muizzu said. Stressing on the close relations between the two countries, he said, “Only two such longstanding friends could have talked so widely and agreed on so much about our future together”. Muizzu said, for him, the talks represented a “clear shared ambition to move the Maldives-Pakistan partnership into a new era”. He said the discussions encompassed several sectors including trade and investment; health and education; environment, fisheries and agriculture; youth and sports; policing and defence; training and capacity-building; and tourism. The Maldivian president said he was pleased about the signing of 20 MoUs. “These memoranda will open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results. Our next step, of course, is to translate these understandings into tangible opportunities and meaningful benefits for the people of both nations.” Muizzu also said he endorsed the goal to take the two countries’ bilateral trade quantum from $13m to $200m in two years. “The Maldives and Pakistan are worlds of untapped potential for each other,” the Maldivian president said. He reaffirmed that the two countries would take a “firm step in the right direction”, adding that Thursday’s business forum would provide an opportunity to bring together business leaders, inventors and innovators from both countries to turn the friendship into mutually beneficial investments. He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well. He further said that the two countries’ leaders saw “considerable potential in halal and Muslim-friendly tourism”. Moreover, Muizzu appreciated Pakistan’s scholarships and placements for Maldivian students, adding that the leaders would broaden the opportunities further, especially in artificial intelligence, digitisation and future technologies as well as health. “We want our next generation to be prepared for the future and be prepared to shape that future.” Muizzu stressed that climate change was “not an abstract environmental concern” for the Maldives, but “it is a direct challenge to our security, our development and our future”. He welcomed cooperation with Pakistan in areas of climate resilience, conservation, sustainable waste management and renewable energy. He thanked PM Shehbaz for his announcement of donations to help the Maldives plant 5m trees in five years. “Our nations share a commitment to advancing common interests through constructive engagements.” He said the Maldives remained committed to revitalising the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, adding that “rebuilding trust, encouraging meaningful dialogue and strengthening mutual understanding are essential to unlocking the full potential of regional cooperation”. He further expressed the Maldives’ “unequivocal and steadfast solidarity” with Palestinians and their “legitimate right to self-determination”. Muizzu also commended Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts “to promote dialogue, de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and a just and lasting peace” in the Middle East. Concluding his remarks, he said, “For 60 years, Pakistan has stood as a trusted friend of the Maldives.” The two countries have now agreed to “build a new era of partnership on the foundations of our six decades of friendship”, he said. The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University Islamabad, with PM Shehbaz noting that the degree recognised Muizzu’s “sagacious and wise leadership and your great public service to your people in the Maldives”. 20 MoUs signed Pakistan and the Maldives signed a series of MoUs aimed at deepening bilateral relations in multiple sectors, including defence, IT, cybersecurity, health, education, social protection, agriculture and tourism, among others. PM Shehbaz and Muizzu were present at the ceremony where representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents. The two countries signed an MoU on cooperation in the fields of information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital skills, and technology and innovation. An MoU was inked to strengthen cooperation in combating illicit trafficking and abuse of narcotic drugs. The two sides also signed an MoU on social protection as well as on health cooperation and between Maldives Food and Drug Authority and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan. Both nations also signed MoUs focused on the recruitment of health professionals, strengthening defence ties and maritime security cooperation. An MoU was signed to boost agriculture cooperation, besides another one on promoting fisheries cooperation. To promote ties in technical and vocational education, an MoU on collaboration to promote technical and vocational education and training was signed, while another MoU was inked to promote educational cooperation. The representatives of Pakistan and the Maldives also exchanged MoUs on cooperation in the field of youth and sports development, air connectivity, tourism and in the field of arts, culture and heritage. The MoUs were signed between the National College of Policy and Law Enforcement of the Maldives Police Service and National Police Academy, Islamabad; Civil Service Commission of Maldives and the Federal Public Service Commission of Pakistan; and Civil Service Commission of Maldives and Civil Service Academy (CSA) of Pakistan. In order to boost commercial engagement, an MoU was signed between the Maldives State Trading Organisation (STO) and Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) for cooperation in trade of agriculture commodities, food and other products, besides signing another pact aimed at boosting cooperation in the field of environment. Prior to the MoU signing ceremony, Muizzi was welcomed at the Prime Minister House with a guard of honour. He held introductions with federal ministers while PM Shehbaz greeted the Maldivian delegation. According to a statement by PM Office (PMO), the prime minister extended a “warm welcome to the esteemed guest”, followed by a guard of honour by smartly turned-out contingents of all three armed forces. The visiting dignitary also planted a sapling at PM House, and prayers were offered for the progress and prosperity of both countries. A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment. President Zardari calls for stronger bilateral economic cooperation President Zardari also met his Maldivian counterpart at the President’s House in Islamabad, where he emphasised the need to translate the political goodwill between the two countries into “greater trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges”. According to a press release by the President’s Secretariat, he also reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to supporting Maldives in education, healthcare, human resource development, social protection and sustainable development. “The two leaders reviewed bilateral relations and discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” the statement said. President Zardari reaffirmed the importance Pakistan attaches to its “longstanding fraternal relations” with the Maldives, highlighting that Muizzu’s state visit coincided with the 60-year anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and provided “fresh momentum” to the bilateral partnership. He also recalled Pakistan’s contributions to the development of the Maldives, including the Parliament building and the School of Medicine in Malé. The press release added that both leaders expressed satisfaction over the positive trajectory of bilateral relations and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in areas of mutual interest. They recognised the disproportionate impact of climate change on vulnerable countries, particularly small island developing states and climate-vulnerable developing economies. “President Zardari expressed Pakistan’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Maldives in climate resilience, environmental protection and sustainable development, including support for President Muizzu’s Five Million Tree Initiative,” the statement said. Additionally, the leaders exchanged views on regional and international developments and underscored the importance of “dialogue, diplomacy, sovereign equality, mutual respect and peaceful resolution of disputes”, it said. They also reaffirmed their support for the rights of the Palestinian people and the establishment of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine. According to the statement, Muizzu was accompanied by Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam; Minister of Defence and National Service Hassan Rasheed; Minister of Homeland Security, Labour and Technology Ali Ihusaan; Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade Mohamed Saeed; and High Commissioner of the Republic of Maldives Mohamed Thoha. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Maritime Minister Junaid Anwar, Senators Sherry Rehman and Saleem Mandviwala, former federal minister MNA Naveed Qamar, the foreign secretary, and the High Commissioner of Pakistan to the Maldives were also present, it added. The meeting was followed by a state banquet hosted by President Zardari in honour of President Muizzu and his accompanying delegation. It was attended, among others, by PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu and Commander National Strategic Command General Syed Aamer Raza. Meeting with Dar Earlier in the day, DPM Dar called on Muizzu, welcoming him and his delegation to Pakistan, the FO said on X. Dar “underscored the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade, investment, education, climate change and tourism”, the FO said. DPM Dar also welcomed the Maldivian business delegation in the Maldives-Pakistan Business Forum and “expressed hope that B2B engagements would yield concrete trade and investment opportunities”. Muizzu, speaking to Dar, “expressed Maldives’ desire to deepen its close relations with Pakistan and explore new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation”, the FO said. Separately, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry held a meeting with Maldivian Minister for Homeland Security Ali Ihusan and exchanged views on enhancing bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries, a statement by the interior ministry said. According to the statement, the two agreed to promote cooperation on immigration and to curb human smuggling and organised crime. It quoted Chaudhry as saying: “Pakistan values sharing experiences and security cooperation with friendly countries to promote peace and stability in the region. Pakistan wants to strengthen bilateral cooperation with the Maldives in the areas of law enforcement and internal security.” He stressed the need for cooperation between the two sides to tackle the challenges of illegal immigration and human smuggling and assured the visiting dignitary on Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s behalf of “all-possible assistance for enhancing bilateral cooperation”. Last month, the Maldives’ parliamentary speaker Abdul Raheem Abdullah met with Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Rawalpindi. In 2015 , former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-PM Nawaz Sharif.

items.title: Milán, una ciudad rota por el lujo y la desigualdad
items.description: Milán es la ciudad a la que la cantante Dua Lipa está pensando irse a vivir pero también donde muchos de sus vecinos se ven obligados a marcharse. Está entre las que acoge más millonarios del mundo, que se instalan en nuevos rascacielos firmados por grandes arquitectos. Llegan atraídos por la tarifa plana fiscal ofrecida en Italia desde 2017, un solo pago de 300.000 euros (convenció a Cristiano Ronaldo a irse del Real Madrid a la Juventus en 2018). Es el llamado modelo Milán , una ciudad de lujo, de cultura, de moda, de bancos de inversión, ideal para vivir, salvo que por el precio de los pisos y de los alquileres vivir se ha vuelto imposible: comprar cuesta un 57% más que hace una década y alquilar, un 70% más que en 2018, según los datos de los portales inmobiliarios. Cerca de 300 afganos han sido expulsados por las autoridades alemanas a su país de origen desde 2025 , desde que tomó posesión el actual Gobierno federal. items.title: Milei agita la campaña con insultos a Sánchez y abrazos a Ayuso
items.description: Cuando se confirmó que Javier Milei volvía a España pero esta vez en plena precampaña electoral, el equipo de campaña del presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, no daba crédito. Parecía un regalo perfecto. Y lo fue. Hasta el alcalde de Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, del PP, admitió que el viaje era un caramelo para el presidente. “Pedro Sánchez será el primero que esté muy feliz por la propaganda que le ha dado Milei hoy, estoy seguro”, llegó a decir el regidor. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El PP confía en que el impacto de la visita de Milei se diluya el 29-N: “Si llega a venir la última semana sería distinto”
items.description: No es la primera vez que sucede. Hace dos años, en junio de 2024, en la anterior visita de Javier Milei a España, Isabel Díaz Ayuso incomodó a Génova al otorgar al presidente de Argentina la medalla internacional de la Comunidad de Madrid, en un acto con toda la pompa del que fue ajeno el líder del PP. Ahora, en plena precampaña electoral, la presencia del histriónico mandatario latinoamericano vuelve a ser incómoda para el PP, salvo para la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, que ha vuelto a reivindicarlo como un referente, al recibirlo calurosamente y exhibir complicidad con un abrazo mientras el líder de su partido lo ignoraba y ponía tierra de por medio con un acto en Sevilla centrado en las políticas de vivienda. Los populares son conscientes de que los insultos de Milei en Madrid a Pedro Sánchez, a quien llamó este miércoles “impresentable dictador”, pueden activar al electorado progresista, pero confían en que el impacto de la visita del presidente argentino se diluya porque aún faltan 40 días para la cita con las urnas. “Menos mal que ha venido ahora y no el 21 de noviembre, porque si llega a venir la última semana de campaña el escenario sería distinto”, admite un dirigente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El abogado de afectados por la ‘ley de nietos’ asume que no podrán votar: “El Constitucional era la única vía posible”
items.description: Antes de que su abogado, Pedro J. Díaz, pudiera darle la noticia, el único ciudadano español nacionalizado al amparo de la ley de nietos que acudió al Tribunal Constitucional para adherirse al recurso de amparo del Defensor del Pueblo ya le había enviado el enlace de la información con el fallo. El pleno del tribunal de garantías había inadmitido, por diez votos a dos, el recurso que reclamaba restablecer el derecho al voto de más de 160.000 nacionalizados, entre ellos el suyo. Junto al enlace, el hombre, español de origen argentino, escribió una pregunta tan breve como cargada de desazón: “¿Y ahora qué se puede hacer?”. El portazo judicial lo dejó triste y desmoralizado, aunque no ha conseguido apagar del todo su esperanza. Su abogado, sin embargo, mira al futuro con mucho menos optimismo. Las posibilidades de que los afectados puedan votar el próximo 29 de noviembre son, a su juicio, “pocas o ninguna”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Qué dice la instrucción de la ‘ley de nietos’ que está bajo la lupa del Supremo?
items.description: La retirada del derecho al voto a más de 160.000 nacionalizados por la llamada ley de nietos ha puesto el foco en una ley y una instrucción aprobadas en octubre de 2022 sin que ningún partido político las recurriera. La Ley de Memoria democrática se publicó en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) el 19 octubre de ese año tras un año de compleja tramitación parlamentaria con intensos debates, no solo entre el Gobierno y la oposición sino también con los socios de investidura. La instrucción del Ministerio de Justicia con las directrices para tramitar el derecho a optar a la nacionalidad española se aprobó seis días después y solo fue impugnada por una asociación contraria a las leyes de memoria histórica y democrática, pero su recurso fue desestimado por una cuestión de forma. Cuatro años después, el debate político a las puertas de un nuevo ciclo electoral ha desenterrado aquella instrucción que en su momento pasó inadvertida para los partidos y ahora ha derivado en un enorme embrollo jurídico. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El avance de Vox en las coaliciones con el PP: de la “nacionalidad española” en la ley de vivienda de Aragón a la censura en Castilla y León
items.description: Este octubre se cumplen seis meses desde que el PP inaugurase la segunda ronda de Gobiernos autonómicos con Vox. María Guardiola, baronesa extremeña, cedía de nuevo ante la extrema derecha incluyéndola en su Ejecutivo y desataba la caída del resto de fichas del dominó: Aragón, Castilla y León y Andalucía. En todas los pactos, los populares dieron cancha a la formación de Santiago Abascal, cuya agenda ultra ha ido avanzando en los boletines territoriales desde entonces hasta hoy. Medidas que se han acelerado con el inicio del curso político, así como con la paulatina aprobación de los Presupuestos autonómicos en plena precampaña de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre en la que, según las encuestas, la alianza de PP y Vox puede alcanzar una mayoría de gobierno. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Móviles plegables: qué ganas, qué pierdes y cuánto duran de verdad
items.description: La expectación ante la llegada del iPhone Duo, que se agotó en reservas online y tiene un plazo de entrega de tres meses, ha vuelto a poner en el centro de la actualidad tecnológica a este tipo de dispositivos. En realidad, la propuesta del primer smartphone plegable de Apple es muy similar a la que hemos visto durante los últimos años en fabricantes como Samsung, Huawei o Motorola: un teléfono que se abre para mostrar una pantalla enorme con la que es posible leer, ver vídeos, consultar documentos o trabajar con varias aplicaciones a la vez de forma más cómoda que con un terminal tradicional. Sin embargo, esa versatilidad tiene un precio, tanto económico como práctico. Las preguntas que muchos se hacen antes de tomar la decisión de adquirirlo son obvias: ¿Merece la pena pagar más por un móvil que se dobla? ¿Es tan delicado como puede parecer? ¿Puede sustituir realmente a una tablet? Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ibai Llanos entra con ‘La velada del año’ en el combate de Netflix por los ‘youtubers’
items.description: Netflix necesita más y más youtubers para que la llama siga ardiendo. Este lunes, la plataforma de streaming anunció que retransmitirá en exclusiva La velada del año de Ibai Llanos hasta 2029 , pero el español es solo el último creador de contenidos de la plataforma de Google al que Netflix ha echado el guante en su estrategia de los últimos meses . Llanos es parte de un engranaje que va mucho más allá. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Sara Carbonero: “Lo que viví en el Mundial de Sudáfrica fue machismo”
items.description: No hay duda de que Sara Carbonero (Corral Almaguer, 42 años) es periodista hasta la médula. Intuye perfectamente cuando un colega busca el titular fácil y también cuándo se enfrenta a preguntas nuevas. Sabe cómo ser cálida poniendo límites. “No es el mejor momento. Mi madre falleció por el mismo tipo de cáncer que el mío. Hay días que me levanto pensando: ‘Por favor, que pase algo bueno’”, explica con dulzura al final de la entrevista. Pero también es una enorme empresaria. Estuvimos con ella en Valencia, en la apertura de su novena tienda Slowlove. “Estamos muy orgullosas porque emprender es durísimo. Nosotras las hemos pasado canutas”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Entre el uniforme y el privilegio: ¿por qué los grandes diseñadores de moda siempre visten igual?
items.description: A primera vista, la escena roza la ironía: tras un despliegue vertiginoso de texturas, volúmenes imposibles, combinaciones audaces y tendencias destinadas a redefinir el vestidor global, la música se apaga y el diseñador sale a saludar a su público entregado. ¿Y qué lleva puesto? Una camiseta gris o negra de corte impecable pero anodino, unos vaqueros rectos y unas zapatillas blancas. Ni rastro del maximalismo o la vanguardia que acaba de desfilar por la pasarela. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Lori Meyers, supervivientes de un ‘indie’ que ya desapareció: “Somos currelas de los festivales”
items.description: Contaba en sus redes sociales el líder de Lori Meyers, Antonio López, Noni (Granada, 45 años), que se habían “cansado de tocar en festivales” y por eso daban el martes 13 de octubre un concierto en la sala El Sol de Madrid para unas 300 personas. El concierto era verdad, pero lo del cansancio era una broma. “Una tontería”, confirmaba él mismo a EL PAÍS en la zona de reservado del mítico local horas antes del recital. Es el primero en 15 años que recuerdan dar en ese formato, es decir, un repertorio completo en una sala de aforo pequeño, cara a cara con su público. En su trayectoria predominan los festivales: más de cien actuaciones en ese tipo de escenarios, del Primavera Sound de 2004 al Benicàssim, Bella Vista o Ebrovisión de este mismo verano. El guitarrista y covocalista, Alejandro Méndez (Granada, 45 años), reconocía tener algo de nervios, “sales de tu zona de confort”, sobre todo en cuanto a cuestiones técnicas. Completa el trío como miembro oficial Alfredo Núñez, batería. Seguir leyendo

items.title: No es por la motosierra
items.description: El bienestar europeo da signos de agotamiento. Mientras en Francia arden las calles, en España habrá una huelga general el 11 de noviembre . Lo curioso es que no son países neoliberales: nuestro Gobierno está batiendo récords de recaudación de impuestos, y el Estado francés destina alrededor de un 60% de su PIB al gasto público , una de las cifras más altas del mundo. La campaña electoral de Pedro Sánchez versa ahora sobre espolear el miedo a la motosierra de las derechas, pero aún con más Estado, ya hay miles de jóvenes europeos que no pueden alcanzar el bienestar esperado o el que sus padres obtuvieron. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Allende el Planeta
items.description: A la medianoche del 15 de octubre de 2026, mientras los reyes Felipe y Letizia le entregaban un trofeo en forma de globo terráqueo y un cheque de un millón de euros ante 4.000 invitados puestos en pie aplaudiéndola durante 10 minutos, los editores de Penguin Random House se enteraban de que Isabel Allende , la reina madre de su catálogo, les dejaba por otra. Por Planeta, concretamente, el gigante de la competencia, a cuyo celebérrimo premio se había presentado Allende anónimamente sin decirles ni media, junto a otros 1.424 escritores, y que, gracias al prodigioso olfato del jurado, había ganado de calle. Acababa así, por las bravas, una relación profesional, y personal, de 44 años que comenzó con la publicación, en 1982, del superventas mundial La casa de los espíritus y siguió con otras 30 obras siempre rentables para todos. Hasta aquí, una de tantas historias de cuernos profesionales, y personales, en los que el cornudo es el último en enterarse. Pero, más allá de guerras editoriales y cálculos de mercado, me interesan las razones íntimas por las que Allende, una mujer de 84 años con la vida resuelta y los suculentos dividendos de sus libros engordándole las arcas cada fin de año, da semejante campanazo. Se me dirá que por dinero, claro, que nunca es suficiente. Por el millón del premio, multiplicado por tres o cuatro, más los derechos del siguiente libro, más equis prebendas, porque cuando se ficha a una grande, se suele fichar el lote, como cuando la muy fina revista ¡Hola! contrata desde la pedida de mano, la boda, la luna de miel, el embarazo, el bautizo y hasta el divorcio de una pareja de famosos, que ahora se divorcian hasta en las mejores familias. Poderosas razones que, sospecho, no explican del todo el volantazo de la chilena. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La banca afronta una factura millonaria al tener que devolver el dinero a sus clientes víctimas de fraude
items.description: El cliente siempre tiene la razón, también en cuestiones relacionadas con fraudes bancarios. La justicia europea ha puesto el punto final a las disputas entre las entidades y las víctimas de fraudes, incluso aunque hayan cometido una negligencia grave, como llevar anotada la clave en la tarjeta de crédito, dictar por teléfono el código de un solo uso o instalar una aplicación de control remoto en el ordenador a solicitud de un desconocido. De entrada, las entidades financieras no podrán aducir ese motivo para denegar la devolución del dinero, como hacían hasta ahora, de acuerdo con una reciente sentencia del Tribunal de Justicia de la Unión Europea (TJUE). Los bancos tendrán que reclamarle, a posteriori, el dinero al cliente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Más de 100 migrantes de Ceuta han recibido el asilo
items.description: En torno a un centenar de migrantes que entraron en Ceuta entre el 30 y el 31 de julio ya tienen la protección internacional que les permite permanecer legalmente en España y les reconoce el derecho a residir y trabajar en el país. Así lo han confirmado a este periódico diversas fuentes internas, que constatan que las resoluciones de asilo concedidas desde el 31 de julio ascienden a 180 expedientes. No obstante, no todas son de migrantes que llegaron a Ceuta en el cruce masivo , sino que algunos de ellos corresponden a personas que ya estaban previamente en la ciudad. Los relativos a las personas que llegaron a finales de julio se cifran en algo más de un centenar. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Frente Amplio sitúa en los puestos de salida por Madrid a los principales partidos de la coalición
items.description: Pasado el folletín del intento frustrado para una única papeleta en la izquierda, Frente Amplio empieza a despejar las incógnitas sobre la configuración de sus listas. La coalición que aúna a una quincena de partidos por todo el país y que tiene como principales referentes a Izquierda Unida, Más Madrid, Comuns y Movimiento Sumar (MS) ha cerrado ya los primeros puestos de la candidatura en Madrid, donde, tras un pulso intenso que mantuvo bloqueado el acuerdo durante días, finalmente estarán todas las fuerzas de Sumar en el Gobierno excepto la catalana Comuns, que acaparará la papeleta por Barcelona, encabezada por la aspirante a la presidencia, Ada Colau. Aunque las encuestas dibujan en este momento una representación de la izquierda muy a la baja respecto a los comicios de 2023, cuando el grupo de Yolanda Díaz obtuvo 31 escaños, el reparto final otorga a la organización de la ministra Mónica García las dos primeras posiciones y la quinta, mientras que la tercera será para IU y la cuarta para MS. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las infecciones sexuales se frenan en España después de una década disparadas
items.description: Las infecciones de transmisión sexual (ITS), que llevaban una década disparadas en España, remitieron en 2025. El último informe del Centro Nacional de Epidemiología (CNE) , que adelanta EL PAÍS, muestra una leve caída de la sífilis y del linfogranuloma venéreo, una estabilización de casos de gonorrea y una subida moderada de clamidia. El documento no refleja el VIH, que se mide en otro informe independiente y que lleva unos años estabilizado. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Sanidad aclara cuándo se puede ingresar a un paciente psiquiátrico contra su voluntad ante la preocupación de los profesionales
items.description: La Ley General de Discapacidad , que entra en vigor este viernes, tiene preocupada a la Sociedad Española de Psiquiatría y Salud Mental (SEPSM). Junto con una veintena de asociaciones autonómicas y especializadas, alerta de que uno de los artículos de la nueva norma podía dejar sin cobertura algunos ingresos involuntarios de pacientes graves. Para aclarar este procedimiento, el Ministerio de Sanidad ha abierto este miércoles una consulta pública previa que desarrollará reglamentariamente ese artículo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La receta de ensalada de atún que le da una vuelta a la mixta de siempre
items.description: La lechuga y el atún o el bonito hacen buena pareja, y eso lo sabemos desde que se inventó la ensalada mixta allá por el Pleistoceno. Nada que objetar a ese clasicazo, que nos ha acompañado en tantísimas comidas y siempre funciona cuando está bien hecho, pero como también estamos por la innovación, reivindicamos a la vez las fórmulas que se salen de lo corriente. Hace unos años ya publicamos tres ensaladas de lechuga que no son la de siempre . Hoy volvemos a la carga con una receta que une esta verdura con sus amigos el bonito y las aceitunas, y la refresca con un aliño de limón y tomillo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Oil rises as US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions
items.description: Oil prices rose on Thursday as more attacks by the Houthis in Saudi ‌Arabia prompted the United States to order some diplomats and family members to leave its missions in the Kingdom. Brent crude futures rose $1.29, or 1.2%, to $110.11 a barrel at 00:34 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude gained 97 cents, or 1%, to $98.12. Brent settled largely unchanged on Wednesday, while WTI eased 67 cents. The Reuters Power Up newsletter, by columnist Ron Bousso, covers everything you need to know about the global energy industry. Sign up here. The US State Department plans to withdraw family members ​from several other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. Yemen’s Iran-aligned ⁠Houthis struck several targets on Wednesday with at least one person killed and eight more wounded at a ​civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oil field. Iranian media reported on Wednesday that explosions were also heard in Sirik in southern Iran, and that the nature and origin of the explosions were unknown. On Wednesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told the Financial Times that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself and President ​Masoud Pezeshkian told state media the US could not expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran. Kpler data showed at least 18 attacks on shipping over the past two weeks, while LSEG analysts warned that Iran was targeting tankers well beyond the Strait of Hormuz, reaching into the Gulf of Oman and jeopardising Gulf crude loadings and ship-to-ship transfers supporting regional loadings. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks on ending the war in Ukraine amid Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The ​Kremlin said Putin had agreed ​to resume US-mediated peace talks ⁠with Ukraine as soon as next month. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he supported the talks and hoped they would start as soon as possible. US crude stocks fell by 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels last week, the US Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for an 820,000-barrel draw. Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose 1.68 million barrels to 104.3 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.16 million-barrel drop, EIA data showed. The Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly a third of the 1-million-barrel US emergency heating oil reserve, the Department of Energy said on Wednesday, to help contain prices that have surged amid diesel shortages driven by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

items.title: Una calle de Madrid como retrato de la vivienda pública: 18 pisos cerrados, 18 oportunidades perdidas
items.description: Camino Alto de San Isidro es una calle peatonal de Carabanchel con alma de corrala. Por las tardes, los adultos se asoman a los balcones y se sientan en sillas plegables a ver pasar a los niños en edades de primaria volando a 25 kilómetros por hora en patinetes eléctricos. Otros pequeños juegan al fútbol cerca de una pared de ladrillo donde alguien pegó hace tiempo una foto de Jenni Hermoso, la estrella del fútbol femenino que dio aquí sus primeras patadas al balón. Los vecinos hablan de chismes y asuntos serios, entre otros un tema que les duele: el problema de los pisos vacíos, cerrados con puertas de acero. Todo el mundo los ha visto en esta colonia de 28 bloques, una de las principales reservas de vivienda pública de la región, donde no es raro que diez o doce personas compartan un mismo hogar. EL PAÍS ha recorrido los edificios uno a uno y ha contado 18 pisos cerrados. Seguir leyendo

items.title: León, el destino sorpresa para 2027: de las vidrieras góticas al Barrio Húmedo
items.description: La ciudad de León se ha colado en la selección de los destinos más interesantes para descubrir en 2027 en todo el mundo, según el ranking anual Best in Travel de Lonely Planet. Los que se animen a visitarla, podrán descubrir que la ciudad tiene unas vidrieras excepcionales en una de las catedrales más bellas de Europa, unos inesperados frescos románicos en San Isidoro, la sorprendente arquitectura de Gaudí , un divertido Barrio Húmedo para probar los mejores vinos de la tierra o un museo contemporáneo de los que llaman la atención. A lo que se suma que la capital está profundamente ligada al Camino de Santiago (y 2027 será nuevamente Año Jacobeo). Definitivamente, 2027 será un buen momento para descubrir o revisitar León. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Islamabad High Court seeks evidence against NAB officials’ appointments
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Wednesday issued notices to the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), the Ministry of Law and other respondents on a petition challenging the appointments of the bureau’s Deputy Chairman Ihtesham Qadir Shah and Prosecutor General Sohail Nasir, while directing the petitioner to produce documentary evidence that the two did not meet the legal requirements for their posts. Justice Umair Majid Malik, who heard the petition filed by Advocate Dr G.M. Chaudhry, observed that the petitioner had “completely ruined the entire case” after he argued that Mr Nasir had improperly described himself as a former judge despite having served only as an additional judge of the Lahore High Court (LHC). Justice Malik remarked with a smile, “In that case, you might as well remove our badges too, as we are also currently serving as additional judges.” ‘Lack qualifications’ In his petition, filed in the nature of quo warranto, Dr Chaudhry challenged the appointments of the NAB deputy chairman and prosecutor general, arguing that Mr Shah did not meet the qualifications prescribed under Section 7(aa) of the National Accountability Ordinance (NAO), 1999. The petitioner contended that Mr Shah had previously served as NAB prosecutor general, a position that did not qualify him as a federal government officer in Grade 21 or its equivalent. He also argued that Mr Shah was neither an armed forces officer holding the rank of major general nor its equivalent. Regarding Mr Nasir, the petitioner argued that he did not meet the criteria under Section 8(a) of the NAO, which requires a NAB prosecutor general to be qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court judge. He said Mr Nasir had served as a sessions judge before being appointed an additional judge of the LHC, but was not confirmed. The petitioner maintained that he therefore did not meet the requirements under Article 177(2) of the Constitution. Notices were also issued on miscellaneous applications seeking to restrain the NAB deputy chairman and prosecutor general from performing their duties and to summon the records of their appointments. Published in Dawn, October 22nd, 2026

Leonoras, las nuevas galletas en honor de la Princesa de Asturias y otros postres reales
items.description: Han trabajado durante dos años para crear unas galletas, bautizadas como Leonoras en honor de la Princesa de Asturias. No son pasteleros ni cocineros, sino ingenieros. José Manuel Monje, de 62 años, nacido en Madrid pero criado en Oviedo y titulado en Ingeniería de Minas, y Enrique Ortea (Oviedo, 49 años), ingeniero mecánico, ambos profesores de la Fundación Masaveu de Formación Profesional, el mismo centro en el que se formaron, han querido rendir homenaje a Leonor de Borbón . “Empezamos a darle vueltas a cómo podíamos rendirle homenaje. Como formadores, vemos en los jóvenes con los que tratamos a diario una falta de valores y pensamos que la Princesa de Asturias podía ser un referente. Nos llama la atención su esfuerzo, responsabilidad, constancia e ilusión, valores que apreciamos cada vez menos entre los jóvenes y que creemos que conviene reivindicar”, explica al otro lado del teléfono Ortea, después de presentar públicamente este dulce en un acto celebrado este martes en la Cámara de Comercio de Oviedo. A su lado está Monje, su compañero en esta aventura, que comenzó durante una conversación de pasillo coincidiendo con la celebración de los Premios Princesa de Asturias. “A los dos nos gusta la repostería y, como decimos en Asturias, somos llambiones (golosos), así que nos decidimos por una pasta florentina crocante, en la que sustituimos la almendra por la avellana para mantener la tradición de nuestra tierra”, prosigue Ortea. Seguir leyendo La reina también tiene sus Letizias Las Leonoras se suman a una larga tradición de productos gastronómicos bautizados con nombres regios. La reina Letizia tampoco es ajena al mundo de la repostería, y menos aún en su tierra. Tiene sus propias pastas, conocidas como Letizias o Corazones de Letizia, creadas en 2004 por el confitero Ángel Ampudia, de la pastelería La Veguina, en Ribadesella, con motivo de la boda de los entonces príncipes de Asturias. Están elaboradas con mantequilla y almendra. Antes llegaron otros dulces inspirados en reinas. Es el caso de las Cristinas, vinculadas a la figura de María Cristina de Borbón, cuarta esposa de Fernando VII y regente durante la minoría de edad de Isabel II. La coca Cristina, típica de la Comunidad Valenciana y elaborada con almendra, alcanzó gran popularidad en el siglo XIX. También están las Cristinas de San Blas, propias de Cataluña y Aragón, similares a los bollos suizos, o las de Jaén, una versión distinta elaborada con manteca de cerdo, aceite de oliva, harina, huevos, ralladura de limón y canela, entre otros ingredientes. Y están las Fabiolas, creadas en homenaje a Fabiola de Mora y Aragón con motivo de su boda con el rey Balduino de Bélgica en 1960. En su honor se bautizó la barra de pan Fabiola, muy popular en Castilla y León, especialmente en Palencia, donde los panaderos adaptaron el tradicional pan candeal a un formato de barra. También lleva su nombre el bizcocho Fabiola, típico de la Comunidad Valenciana, especialmente de Altea, y presente asimismo en Cataluña. Se trata de un bizcocho jugoso, bañado en almíbar y elaborado con coco rallado y almendra.

items.title: Meta strikes deal to keep Zuckerberg in California after wealth tax concerns
items.description: Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him in California after the CEO warned he was considering leaving the state that houses the company’s headquarters if voters pass a wealth tax proposal next month. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares he can sell to potentially cover a multi-billion-dollar tax bill if the proposal passes, in exchange for committing to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday. Zuckerberg, the world’s sixth-richest person according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Proposition 40, a ballot measure dubbed the “California wealth tax”, could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. Proposition 40, which asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, is far from certain to pass, political ​analysts say. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth ​upwards of $2 trillion. Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20% of ‌the Class ⁠C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill without losing voting control. The company said on Wednesday it will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively creating ​a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg’s control. Meta’s long-term forecasts, as described in the filing, showed it would need to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years, beginning as early as fall 2026, to finance its AI-related growth plan. Facebook and Instagram’s parent company said a special committee of its board concluded it was “critically ⁠important” that Zuckerberg remain in a leadership role and continue to manage the company from its California headquarters, particularly during what it described as an “unprecedented challenge and competition in ​our industry” driven by AI.

items.title: Tesla aims to sell Cybercab robotaxis by end of year despite federal probe
items.description: Tesla ​is aiming to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of this year, its ‌engineering chief said on Wednesday, even as the US auto safety agency probes the vehicles that come without manual controls, which federal regulations typically require. The gold, two-seaters – that come with butterfly doors and drive themselves without any steering wheel, pedals or mirrors – are one of the key bets CEO Elon ​Musk has made in his ambition of turning the EV maker into an AI and robotics company. The Auto File newsletter brings you exclusive insights on the biggest shifts driving the global automotive industry. Sign up here. “As Tesla grows, we’ll ​mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercabs will be the first,” Lars Moravy, ⁠Tesla’s vice president of vehicle engineering, told analysts after reporting third-quarter results. “We’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end ​of this year, 2026,” he said. “As we start small this year, and we learn … about delivery and ownership and fleet management of ​autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.” After years of missed promises by Musk, Tesla started offering paid rides on a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin, Texas, early last month amid a frenzy of fans and social media influencers. Just hours later, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said ​it opened an investigation into Cybercabs to assess how Tesla determined the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations. Those regulations, written decades ago for ​human-driven vehicles, require manual controls and limit commercial deployment of vehicles that are designed without them. Unlike most other countries, where new vehicle models and technology need regulatory clearance before launch, automakers in the US can deploy them on public roads by self-certifying that they meet federal standards. NHTSA declined to comment. The agency said last month it was reviewing the basis for Tesla’s certification of the Cybercab and how the company determined that certain standards did not apply to the vehicle. Tesla has until October 30 to ​respond to the agency. NHTSA has proposed changes to federal safety standards to allow AVs designed without human controls. Until those changes are complete, NHTSA said existing standards remain in force. SCALING THE CYBERCAB “I think the key thing which we are trying ​to make sure is that we have all the regulatory approvals where we can start deploying ​the Cybercabs as ⁠fast as we can produce them,” Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI, said on the call. That aside, “scaling would not be that much of a challenge,” he said, adding that the Cybercab was “one of the easiest products” to scale in terms of manufacturing. The Cybercab is part of ⁠Tesla’s robotaxi ​network that includes autonomous Model Ys, some with human safety monitors. Over time, Tesla intends to make the Cybercab the main driverless vehicle model in a larger robotaxi network. Tesla plans to expand the Cybercab service to Dallas next month, Elluswamy ​said. The vehicle, however, will mainly be Tesla owned and used for its ride-hailing service, Musk said.

items.title: Remove barriers to digital work, Bright Simons urges government
items.description: Vice-President in charge of research at IMANI Centre for Policy and Education, Bright Simons, has urged government to remove barriers that prevent ordinary Ghanaians from earning a living through digital platforms. Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he warned that poorly designed licensing requirements could obstruct opportunities in the digital economy. Mr Simons pointed to ride-hailing, food delivery and online content creation as examples of activities people had learned without extensive formal training. “When you look at Uber and all the ride-sharing apps and all the e-commerce apps, a lot of the people that have benefited are ordinary people.” He said users had figured out how to navigate mapping services, locate customers and deliver food. He argued their experience showed why policy must also focus on removing obstacles to work. “I’m a big believer in the fact that when it comes to those kinds of things, typically the government is an impediment rather than an enabler.” Mr Simons recalled resisting proposals to impose licensing requirements and local government obligations on ride-hailing services, including Uber and Bolt. He also cited the public reaction to proposed licences for developers in Ghana. He warned against introducing requirements without carefully considering their effects. “So we have to think about policy as also to include the things that remove barriers and bottlenecks for ordinary people,” he said. For Mr Simons, the ability of ordinary people to acquire useful digital skills was already visible in everyday life. He pointed to WhatsApp users and YouTube creators as examples. “Who builds schools to teach people how to use WhatsApp? Who builds schools to teach influencers how to do YouTube influencing?” He said some content creators had achieved significant recognition through skills developed outside formal training programmes. His argument placed the practical effects of regulation at the centre of the discussion. He maintained that supporting ordinary people also meant identifying the restrictions standing in their way. Mr Simons rejected suggestions that examining those restrictions amounted to an abstract policy debate. “Often they are impediments and bottlenecks in their way, and people like us who point them out should not be seen as discussing theory. It’s very practical.”
