items.title: Only 108 of 39,000 underage candidates meet JAMB criteria
items.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Only 108 of about 39,000 underage candidates who sat the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) have met the Federal Government’s screening requirements for possible admission into tertiary institutions. The candidates emerged from a multi-stage assessment designed to determine whether exceptionally young applicants possess the academic ability and psychological, emotional and intellectual maturity required for university education. The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, disclosed this on Wednesday in Abuja while receiving the two highest-scoring candidates and six other top-performing underage candidates in the 2026 UTME, presented by the Registrar of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB), Professor Segun Aina. Alausa said the screening process was intended to ensure that opportunities for exceptionally gifted children did not come at the expense of their preparedness for higher education. According to him, 2,244,149 candidates registered for the 2026 UTME, while 2,174,396 sat the examination. Approximately 39,000 of those who sat the examination were below the prescribed minimum admission age of 16. The minister explained that candidates seeking exemption from the age requirement had to satisfy several conditions, beginning with a minimum UTME score of 320 out of 400, representing 80 per cent. They were also required to score at least 80 per cent in their post-UTME examinations, meet the stipulated 80 per cent threshold in the assessment of their O’level results and pass a screening exercise to establish their psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education. Alausa disclosed that only 391 underage candidates scored at least 320 in the UTME, with further assessments reducing the number eligible for possible admission to 108. He described the successful candidates as exceptionally gifted, noting that they represented approximately 0.005 per cent of those who sat the examination. “You are the geniuses in our society,” the minister told the candidates, stressing that the government had a responsibility to identify exceptional talents and nurture them into innovators capable of developing solutions to Nigeria’s challenges and those of the wider world. Alausa said the minimum admission age of 16 was not intended to frustrate academically gifted children or deny them opportunities to advance, but to ensure that those admitted at a younger age possessed the maturity required to cope with university life. He said feedback from the screening exercise had been encouraging, particularly regarding the candidates’ confidence, intellectual abilities and responses to questions designed to assess their preparedness for higher education. According to him, academic performance alone could not determine whether a child was ready for tertiary education, which also demands emotional stability and the ability to navigate social and intellectual challenges. The minister urged the successful candidates to regard their abilities as a responsibility to society rather than merely an opportunity to secure early admission and personal advancement. “You are the ones that will change Nigeria and change the world with your innovations,” he said. Alausa linked the development of exceptional young talents to Nigeria’s broader prospects, arguing that the country’s youthful population represented a major resource that must be properly educated and harnessed. He put Nigeria’s population at an estimated 220 million, with an average age of 18.5 years, adding that about 70 per cent of the population was below 30. The minister said the Federal Government’s education reforms were designed to expand opportunities for young Nigerians and strengthen the country’s capacity to turn their potential into innovations and solutions that could improve lives. He congratulated the candidates on behalf of President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Ministry of Education, expressing confidence that their abilities could translate into breakthroughs capable of benefiting millions of people. The eight recognised candidates, including the two highest scorers in the 2026 UTME, received plaques and certificates from the minister. Owoeye Daniella Jesudunsin emerged as the highest-scoring candidate with 372 marks, while Enwere Kingsley Ikenna followed with 370. items.title: Police arrest three suspects, recover gun in Jigawa
items.description: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse The Jigawa State Police Command has arrested three suspects and recovered a locally fabricated pistol, ammunition and other weapons along the Nguru–Birniwa Road. The command’s spokesperson, SP Lawan Shiisu Adam, confirmed the arrests in a statement made available to journalists. He said operatives of Operation Salama apprehended the suspects on October 14, 2026, at about 4.30 p.m. during a security patrol. The suspects were identified as Bello Juli, 22; Abdullahi Yakubu, 30; and Bashir Muhammad, 25. All three are from Kyarana Settlement in Kiru Local Government Area of Kano State. According to the police spokesperson, items recovered during the operation included a locally fabricated pistol, three bullets, machetes, bows and arrows, and gunpowder. Adam said the suspects had been charged to court following investigations by the State Criminal Investigation Department in Dutse. Meanwhile, the Commissioner of Police, CP Tijjani Murtala, commended the officers involved in the operation and urged personnel across the command to strengthen surveillance and intelligence gathering to combat criminal activities. He also appealed to members of the public to support security agencies by providing timely information about suspicious individuals and activities in their communities. The command assured residents of its continued commitment to maintaining peace and security across Jigawa State. items.title: Meta fined $25bn for ‘lies’ over user data privacy
items.description: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices. A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data. “The lies extend beyond Facebook’s data practices as well,” the judge said, adding they went to “the heart of Facebook’s core business practices”. Meta’s head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it “all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico”. The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful. The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety. New Mexico’s lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal. That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time. New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Mahoney added. Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user’s permission, when in reality it had been. They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta’s dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times. “For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.” The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter. He said Meta’s violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were “willful” and spanned “more than 11 years”, stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were “designed to mislead the public”, Judge Mathew wrote in his order. While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine. It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices. New Mexico has been one of Meta’s most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children. The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being “the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children”. As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta’s consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. “Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy,” Zuckerberg said. To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn. The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn – an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever. Meta’s revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn. Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta’s chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock. Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use “more funding flexibility” next year.

items.title: EFCC chairman, Mbah, Umahi to grace Enugu NUJ Press Week
items.description: By Anayo Okoli ENUGU — The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Ola Olukoyede; Enugu State Governor, Peter Mbah; and the Minister of Works, David Umahi, are among the dignitaries expected at the grand finale of the 2026 Press Week of the Enugu State Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) on Wednesday. The event, scheduled to hold at the Lawrence Ugwuanyi Press Centre, Enugu, will feature discussions on responsible journalism, democratic development and the media’s role in the fight against corruption. Umahi will deliver the guest lecture, while Olukoyede will give the keynote address at the ceremony, which is expected to attract media professionals, government officials, political leaders, security chiefs and other stakeholders. In a statement signed by the Chairman and Secretary of the Press Week Organising Committee, Emma Ugwueze and Damian Duruiheoma, respectively, the committee said the topics were carefully selected to address critical issues affecting the country. It said Umahi and Olukoyede were chosen in recognition of their respective roles in public service, particularly the minister’s efforts in road infrastructure development and the EFCC chairman’s leadership of the country’s anti-corruption campaign. “While Engr. David Umahi, the Honourable Minister of Works, is making visible efforts towards the rehabilitation and revitalisation of several roads across the country, the EFCC Chairman, Olukoyede, has also introduced reforms aimed at strengthening the operations of the anti-graft commission,” the statement said. Umahi’s lecture will focus on the theme, “Strengthening Democracy Through Responsible Journalism: 2027 Polls in Focus,” while Olukoyede will speak on “The Role of the Media and Other Critical Stakeholders in Sustaining the Fight Against Corruption.” The former Enugu State Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Chief Anthony Ani, SAN, will chair the event. Among those expected to receive awards are the Deputy National Chairman (South) of the All Progressives Congress, Dr Ben Nwoye; the Executive Director of the Projects Development Institute (PRODA), Enugu, Dr Peter Okwudilichukwu Ogbobe; and the Enugu State Commissioner of Police, CP Mamman Bitrus Giwa. Others are the Commissioner representing Enugu State at the Federal Character Commission, Peter Eze; the General Manager of Rangers International Football Club, Amobi Ezeaku; and medical expert Dr Celestine Chijioke Ugwuoke, among other recipients. The grand finale will conclude a series of activities organised by the chapel to mark the 2026 Press Week. The programme commenced on Sunday, October 18, with a thanksgiving service at the Christian Victory Prayer Ministry, popularly known as Precious Church, in Enugu. Other activities included a football match and humanitarian outreach to vulnerable children. The post EFCC chairman, Mbah, Umahi to grace Enugu NUJ Press Week appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana must build its own email services to address US data concerns – Bright Simons
items.description: IMANI Centre for Policy and Education Vice-President and Head of Research Bright Simons says concerns about US access to Ghanaian data would require the country to build its own email services. Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he pointed to the use of foreign email platforms as a challenge for those seeking greater control over their information. “So if we’re worried about our data being exposed to the U.S. government, then we have to literally build our own email services because already the U.S. government sees everything that you put on Gmail or any of those things.” Simons made the claim while discussing data exposure and the policy choices surrounding digital services. He also urged policymakers to remove obstacles that prevent ordinary people from benefiting from technology. Drawing on ride-hailing and delivery services, he said many users had acquired practical digital skills without formal training. “The second point is that when you look at Uber and all the ride-sharing apps and all the e-commerce apps, a lot of the people that have benefited are ordinary people. Nobody taught them how to use mapping services.” He said people had learnt to use geolocation and mapping tools to deliver food and support other commercial activities. For Simons, such experiences should shape how government approaches the digital economy. He argued that regulation could obstruct opportunities when obligations were introduced without sufficient consideration of their effects. “I’m a big believer in the fact that when it comes to those kinds of things, typically the government is an impediment rather than an enabler.” He recalled opposing attempts to impose licensing requirements and local government obligations on ride-hailing platforms such as Uber and Bolt. He also cited the public backlash over proposed licensing requirements for developers in Ghana as evidence that policy decisions have practical consequences. “So we have to think about policy as also to include the things that remove barriers and bottlenecks for ordinary people,” he said. Simons pointed to the widespread use of WhatsApp and the growth of YouTube creators as further examples of people developing digital capabilities outside formal classrooms. “Who builds schools to teach people how to use WhatsApp? Who builds schools to teach influencers how to do YouTube influencing?” He maintained that identifying regulatory obstacles was essential to making technology useful to ordinary people. “Often they are impediments and bottlenecks in their way, and people like us who point them out should not be seen as discussing theory. It’s very practical.”

items.title: 2027: Ebonyi opposition must unite against godfatherism — Ezeh
items.description: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The Labour Party candidate for Abakaliki/Izzi Federal Constituency, Dr Ezeh Emmanuel Ezeh, has urged opposition political parties in Ebonyi State to unite ahead of the 2027 general elections to challenge what he described as political godfatherism and the concentration of power among a privileged few. Ezeh accused influential political actors in the state of treating public offices, government institutions and state resources as private possessions. The Oxford-trained entrepreneur and public affairs commentator made the call in a statement in which he criticised what he described as the concentration of political power, patronage and opportunities among a privileged circle of individuals and their families. He alleged that some political stakeholders had turned public service into an avenue for advancing personal interests at the expense of ordinary citizens grappling with economic difficulties. “Ebonyi is gradually becoming a state held hostage by a small but very self-serving prebendal political elite that has transformed public office into private property and political power into family inheritance,” he said. The Labour Party candidate expressed concern over what he described as the growing influence of political godfathers in determining access to elective positions, alleging that some prominent politicians were securing political offices for their children and positioning them for higher responsibilities. He warned that such practices, if left unchecked, could undermine democratic competition, weaken public accountability and restrict political opportunities to people with established connections to the political establishment. Ezeh also criticised what he characterised as a patronage-driven system in which public contracts and political appointments were allegedly distributed as personal favours rather than on the basis of merit, transparency and the public interest. He questioned the credibility of political stakeholders who convene meetings and zoning summits to discuss the state’s political future without, in his assessment, adequately addressing accountability for governance failures. According to him, Ebonyi’s central challenge goes beyond competition among political parties to what he described as the consolidation of power within a privileged class increasingly detached from the concerns of ordinary citizens. With the 2027 elections approaching, Ezeh urged opposition parties to set aside personal ambitions and internal divisions to build a common platform capable of offering voters a credible alternative. “If Ebonyi is to be saved, the rescue mission will not come from the very people who created the crisis,” he said. He argued that meaningful political change would require a departure from what he described as the politics of inheritance, patronage and elite capture. However, Ezeh cautioned that opposition parties must also demonstrate credibility and a genuine commitment to reform, warning that a change in political leadership without corresponding changes in governance practices could leave the underlying problems unresolved. Ezeh is a former Deputy President of the South-East Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (SECCIMA) and the current President of the Ebonyi Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (EBCCIMA). items.title: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November
items.description: From an awards-tipped role for Andrew Scott to another Hunger Games prequel, here are the films to watch at the cinema and stream at home this month. 1. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth Cliff Booth was the laidback stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019). Pitt won a best supporting actor Oscar for his performance, and Tarantino liked the character so much that he has written him a spin-off comedy-thriller. That’s surprising enough, given that Tarantino isn’t known for sequels – but a bigger surprise is that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is directed by David Fincher (Fight Club, The Social Network). That makes this the first film to be scripted by Tarantino and directed by someone else since From Dusk Till Dawn back in 1996. It’s set in 1977, a time when Cliff Booth is employed to clean up Hollywood’s messes. His latest clients include a talent agent (Elizabeth Debicki) and a TV actor (Scott Caan) who are mixed up with gangsters. “What was once a fairytale is now a crime story,” says the film’s official synopsis, “a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in LA.” Released on 25 November in the UK, the US and Canada 2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping It’s been more than a decade since Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen triumphed in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2 , but audiences are still hungry for more. The first Hunger Games prequel, subtitled The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, was a hit in 2023. And now there’s a sequel to that prequel, which is set 40 years after Songbirds and Snakes and 24 years before Katniss’s adventures. Confused? Us too, but it’ll all make sense to anyone who is already a fan of Suzanne Collins’s bestselling dystopian novels. Sunrise on the Reaping stars Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson’s character from the original films, and Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, who was played by Donald Sutherland. Other younger incarnations include Jesse Plemons as Philip Seymour Hoffman’s character, Kieran Culkin as Stanley Tucci’s, and Elle Fanning as Elizabeth Banks’s. Released on 19 and 20 November internationally 3. Elsinore In 1989, Daniel Day-Lewis was playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre when the pressure got too much for him, and he walked off the stage. It was his last ever theatre performance. His replacement was Ian Charleson, who had starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire a few years earlier. Charleson had Aids, a condition that was fatal at the time, but he was determined to take on the greatest and most demanding stage role of all before he died. In Elsinore, Charleson is played by Andrew Scott, with Olivia Colman as his doctor and Billie Piper as his best friend. Directed by Simon Stone (The Dig) and written by Stephen Beresford (Pride), the film is heart-rending yet joyous – and Scott is sure to be Oscar-nominated. “I wept like a baby,” says Nick Howells in The Standard . “This is a performance of a lifetime, and one the Academy voters would need a collective bout of insanity to ignore.” Released on 20 November in the US, 25 November in France and 29 January in the UK and Ireland 4. Club Kid Jordan Firstman, the comedian and actor best known as Charlie in HBO’s I Love LA, has made one of the most acclaimed films of the year, a festival favourite with a 100% score on the Rotten Tomatoes reviews aggregator site. As well as writing and directing Club Kid, Firstman stars as Peter, a gay club promoter who organises New York’s wildest parties with his business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingne). But after a decade of this drug-fuelled lifestyle, Peter is feeling old and jaded. It’s then that he meets Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the 10-year-old British son he never knew he had. Wendy Ide in Screen Daily says that Firstman’s “joyous, raw comedy drama” is “a crowd-pleasing triumph – an acidic, spikily funny portrait of New York’s hedonistic gay scene which celebrates empathy, community and the unconditional love between a father and his son”. Released on 4 November in France, 6 November in the US and 13 November in Canada 5. Hexed Disney’s most recent animated films have been sequels and prequels – Moana 2 , Mufasa: The Lion King , Zootopia 2 (aka Zootropolis 2) – but the studio is having another crack at new material with Hexed. Its typically plucky heroine is Billie (voiced by Hailee Steinfeld), a suburban teenager who discovers that she was born with magical powers. She then learns the art of sorcery after she is zapped through a portal to Hogwarts – sorry, Hexe – a mysterious realm of witches and enchanted creatures voiced by Jodie Foster, Tracey Ullman, Stephen Fry and Dan Stevens. Hexed isn’t the only cartoon to explore magical worlds this month, either: an animated adaptation of Dr Seuss’s The Cat in the Hat is in cinemas on 5 November. Released on 25, 26 and 27 November internationally 6. Focker-in-Law The Devil Wears Prada 2 was a box-office hit earlier this year. Will another legacy sequel to a 2000s comedy classic have the same appeal? Sixteen years after the third instalment of the Meet the Parents franchise, and 26 years after the first, Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro are back as the neurotic Greg Focker and his disapproving father-in-law, Jack. Three more of the usual suspects are back, too: Owen Wilson, Blythe Danner and Teri Polo as Greg’s wife Pam. (Alas, there’s no sign of Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman, who played Greg’s parents in the last two films.) New cast-members include Beanie Feldstein as Greg and Pam’s daughter, Skyler Gisondo as their son, and, most importantly, Ariana Grande as their son’s fiancée. The twist this time is that Jack welcomes the newcomer into his “circle of trust”, while Greg is the one who has his doubts. Released on 25, 26 and 27 November internationally 7. I Play Rocky When Sylvester Stallone was an aspiring actor in the 1970s, he decided to write himself his dream role, so he bashed out the screenplay for Rocky in three-and-a-half days. Studio executives loved it, but they saw it as a vehicle for Clint Eastwood or Charles Bronson, rather than some unknown wannabe with a mumbly voice. But Stallone wouldn’t sell out – which explains the title of this behind-the-scenes drama: I Play Rocky. Anthony Ippolito stars as the young Sly, alongside Matt Dillon as his father, AnnaSophia Robb as his first wife, and Stephan James as Carl Weathers (Apollo Creed in Rocky). Directed by Peter Farrelly (Green Book / Dumb and Dumber), the true-life underdog story is “stirring, inspiring, surprisingly hilarious and easy to love”, says Johnny Oleksinski in the New York Post . “And refreshingly, it’s not reverential or museumish, but created in the off-beat, tenacious, can-do spirit of Rocky.” Released on 6 November in the UK, the US and Canada 8. Wild Horse Nine Martin McDonagh’s The Banshees of Inisherin was nominated for eight Oscars (including four different acting awards). His new film is tipped to do similarly well, with its star, John Malkovich, being an almost-certain best actor nominee. He and Sam Rockwell play a pair of buffoonish CIA agents having a short holiday on Easter Island. Like the bickering best friends in The Banshees of Inisherin and In Bruges, they share some wonderfully eccentric dialogue and some scenes of explosive violence, but Wild Horse Nine is distinguished by its hard-edged political commentary and by Malkovich’s character’s regrets. McDonagh’s “latest could be the best yet”, says Phil de Semlyen in Time Out , “a bittersweet hangout film about lonely, crumpled men facing up to mortality, dealing with the consequences of violence and chewing the fat to outlandishly funny effect.” Released on 4, 5 and 6 November internationally 9. Being Heumann Siân Heder is the writer-director of Coda, which won the Oscar for best picture in 2022. Her follow-up, Being Heumann, is another inspiring drama featuring disabled actors. It’s drawn from the autobiography of Judith Heumann, a US disability rights activist. In 1977, she and a group of protesters occupied the San Francisco Federal Building because equal rights regulations were being ignored. Mark Ruffalo plays the government official who wants to kick her out, and Ruth Madeley, a wheelchair user herself, stars as Heumann. “The remarkable thing about the British actress’s performance is that she makes us embrace a character so fiery and flawed and exasperatingly unrelenting,” says Steve Pond in The Wrap . “There’s no question that [Heder has] pulled off another crowd-pleasing film, but the key to Being Heumann is that its importance goes beyond those audience smiles.” Released on 6 November in cinemas in the UK, the US and Canada, and on 13 November on Apple TV+ 10. Josephine Kate Erbland in IndieWire calls Josephine a “stunning film… [that I will] heartily recommend and never, ever watch again”. That’s fair enough: Beth de Araújo’s drama is gripping, intelligent, groundbreaking and important, but it’s not exactly a pleasure to watch. It’s the story of an eight-year-old girl (Mason Reeves) who is in a San Francisco park one Sunday morning with her father (a career-best Channing Tatum). They lose sight of each other for a few minutes – and during that time the girl witnesses a brutal sexual assault. The questions now are: How will this horrific experience affect her? How can her father and mother (Gemma Chan) help her? And does she have a responsibility to testify in court? Erbland says that “De Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability”. Released on 20 November in the UK, the US and Ireland, and on 27 November in Canada 11. All of a Sudden Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Drive My Car was one of the sensations of the 2022 Academy Awards: it didn’t just win the best international feature prize, but was nominated for best picture, best director and best adapted screenplay, too. His quirky follow-up, Evil Does Not Exist, made less of an impression, but his deeply humane new film, All of a Sudden, is another awards contender. Virginie Efira plays the manager of a care home for the elderly in Paris. Tao Okamoto plays a Japanese theatre director who is visiting the city. The women’s friendship deepens over the course of a three-hour drama which is “a gentle and infinitely tender exercise on life and death, full of immersive, philosophical musings that wash over our souls”, says Tomris Laffly in Elle . “Patient and tranquil, All of a Sudden feels like a meditation that transforms a viewer into a better version of themselves.” Released on 25 November in the US 12. Paper Tiger Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver and Miles Teller are on top form in Paper Tiger, another gritty, New York-based crime drama from James Gray (Little Odessa, The Yards, We Own the Night). Echoing events from the writer-director’s own childhood, it’s set in the borough of Queens in 1986. Johansson and Teller play Hester and Irwin, a happily married, successful-enough couple with two sons. Driver plays Irwin’s brother Gary, a flashy ex-cop with political connections and charisma to burn. He brings his brother in on a scheme to clean up a polluted canal for a group of Russian immigrants. What with Irwin’s engineering know-how and his own street-smart confidence, Gary reasons, the deal can’t go wrong. But, of course, it can go very wrong indeed, what with the Russians being ruthless gangsters. “As with his finest work, Gray strikes a beautiful balance between fraught interpersonal drama and nail-biting thrills,” says Nick Schager in The Daily Beast . “Paper Tiger pulsates with heart, rancour, and terror.” Released on 13 November in the US and Canada

items.title: Think about how we sign these agreements – Sam George warns over health data
items.description: Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations Minister Sam Nartey George has urged closer scrutiny of agreements involving Ghana’s health records. The Ningo-Prampram MP is warning that assurances from foreign technology companies may not guarantee control over sensitive data. Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he questioned whether contractual promises could protect Ghana’s information from access under foreign laws. His warning comes as Ghana disagrees with the United States over data-sharing provisions in a proposed health compact. “The last point I just want to make is about the use of foreign resources and even the perception of a tailored arrangement that gives you sovereignty over your data,” he said. “That is a mirage that is sold to many African companies, not just Ghanaian companies.” Mr George said his concerns had prompted exchanges with Google and Amazon Web Services over the protections offered in their agreements. “So I’ve had this back and forth with Google and Amazon Web Services, where they give you all kinds of agreements that say you are protected and data sovereign.” He argued that the US CLOUD Act could override assurances made by private technology companies. He linked that concern directly to how Ghana’s health information is handled. He urged decision-makers to examine both the agreements they sign and the platforms they use. “Especially when you look at what they try to do with our health records, extremely important that we begin to think about how we sign this agreement and how we utilise those platforms.” Ghana rejected the proposed US health compact after raising concerns about health data, financing obligations and regulatory authority. President John Mahama said the terms included access to Ghana’s pathogen profile and medical records. The US Embassy disputed the suggestion that Washington sought identifiable patient records. It said the proposed arrangement required aggregate health data without personally identifiable information, mainly to assess health programmes. The proposed compact involved $109 million in US assistance over five years. Mahama later said Washington had requested further discussions on the contested clauses, with a view to amending or removing them.

items.title: Protection, Not Prosecution: Why Nigeria must decriminalise attempted suicide
items.description: By Angela Uwandu Uzoma-Iwuchukwu The National Suicide Prevention Bill, 2026 offers the Senate an opportunity to align Nigerian law with its human rights obligations and with the evidence on suicide prevention. That opportunity should not be lost. On 13 October 2026, the Senate passed the National Suicide Prevention Bill, 2026 (SB. 730) on second reading. During the debate, the Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio, opposed the bill’s central reform, reportedly stating: “If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail.” The remark has understandably drawn public concern. More importantly, it reflects a view that still underpins our criminal law: that a person who survives a suicide attempt should be met with punishment rather than care. From a human rights perspective, that position is difficult to reconcile with Nigeria’s constitutional and international obligations. As the bill moves to committee, it is worth setting out why. An inconsistent legal framework When a human being reaches a point of acute psychological anguish where they attempt to end their life, the immediate imperative of any just, constitutional state must be protection, not prosecution. Yet, for decades, Nigeria’s statutory legal framework has treated deep personal crisis as a criminal act. Under Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code, individuals who survive a suicide attempt face up to one year in prison (both provisions derive from colonial-era legislation; the United Kingdom repealed the equivalent offence through the Suicide Act 1961). This punitive approach creates a stark legal contradiction with the National Mental Health Act, which rightly recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring medical care and psychosocial support. Nigerian law therefore currently treats the same individual as both a patient in need of urgent care and an offender liable to prosecution. The recent advancement of a bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide and establish a national framework for suicide prevention, which passed its second reading in the Senate this week, marks a critical legislative watershed. Sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong (Cross River South), the bill placed a fundamental human rights question before the nation: when a Nigerian survives a suicide attempt, should the state’s first response be prosecution or protection? The bill resolves this inconsistency. Clause 18 repeals both provisions. Part II sets out the rights of persons who have attempted suicide, including confidentiality, informed consent, access to legal representation and protection from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The bill also provides for a Suicide Prevention Unit, national and state surveillance systems, 24-hour crisis helplines and mandatory training for health workers, law enforcement and correctional personnel. The bill drew support from several senators. Senator Dayo Faduyile, a medical doctor, noted that some survivors have subsequently died by suicide while in detention. The bill has been referred to the Committees on Health and on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters for a public hearing. Nigeria’s human rights obligations The question is not solely one of health policy. Nigeria has accepted binding obligations that bear directly on it. UN Special Rapporteurs on the right to health and on torture have found the criminalisation of suicide attempts inconsistent with these obligations, noting that the detention of persons in acute distress may engage the prohibition of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The World Health Organization identifies decriminalisation as a critical step towards the Sustainable Development Goal target of reducing suicide mortality by one third by 2030. From an international human rights and legal standpoint, penalising attempted suicide is fundamentally flawed, counterproductive, and inconsistent with Nigeria’s treaty obligations under international law. Criminalisation undermines the right to health and life As a State party to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, Nigeria must respect, protect and fulfil the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health under Article 12. This includes removing legal and practical barriers to care. A law that deters people from seeking emergency treatment is such a barrier. Instead of deterring suicide, punitive laws actively discourage people from seeking timely mental health interventions and incentivise individuals to ensure their attempts are fatal to avoid imprisonment. A violation of human dignity Subjecting a person surviving severe mental or emotional trauma to handcuffs, detention cells, and trial is a clear affront to human dignity under Section 34 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) and Article 5 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. Incarceration exacerbates psychological suffering, stripping individuals of their agency at their most vulnerable moment rather than providing therapeutic care. Distortion of public health data and interventions. Decriminalisation is a prerequisite for effective public health governance. When suicide attempts are illegal, official data severely underreports the true scale of the mental health crisis in Nigeria. Accurate data is essential to design targeted suicide prevention strategies, establish crisis helplines, train emergency responders, and allocate adequate health sector budgets. The evidence on criminalisation World Health Organization estimates cited during the Senate debate place suicide deaths in Nigeria at approximately 16,000 per year. Practitioners regard this as a conservative figure, since fear of prosecution and stigma lead families to conceal both attempts and deaths. Overcoming the misconception of deterrence Arguments suggesting that criminal sanctions act as a “deterrent” against suicide stem from a fundamental misunderstanding of mental health dynamics and international human rights principles. Suicidal behaviour is not a calculated criminal offence; it is an indicator of unaddressed psychological distress, socio-economic hardship, or deep-seated trauma. Countries across the world that have repealed legacy criminal provisions and replaced them with evidence-based mental health support, crisis response systems, and mandatory psychosocial assessment have seen improved mental health outcomes without an increase in suicide rates. Federal and state competence The Senate President and the Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, raised legitimate questions about the bill’s application across states, given that the Penal Code operates as state law in the North. This is a matter for careful drafting and consultation, not a reason for delay. The National Assembly should lead, and State Houses of Assembly should be engaged to undertake corresponding reforms. The path forward: transforming legislative debate into legal legacy As the bill moves to the Committees on Health and on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters for public hearings and stakeholder engagement, Nigerian lawmakers must prioritise constitutional rights, international standards, and public health over archaic penal logic. Decriminalisation does not mean the state is indifferent to suicide; rather, it shifts the state’s response from the criminal justice system to the public health framework. To build a comprehensive protective framework, Nigeria needs to: Repeal Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code in full, without substituting any alternative sanction, to align national legislation with the National Mental Health Act. Establish national prevention pathways: fund operational crisis helplines, community mental health care, and specialised training for law enforcement officers, teachers, and healthcare workers to serve as first responders. Decriminalisation without accessible care would be incomplete. Guarantee rights-based mental healthcare: Ensure that mental health interventions are accessible, voluntary, non-discriminatory, and rooted in human dignity. Involve the states: Invite State Houses of Assembly to the public hearing and agree to a framework for corresponding reform of state criminal laws. Hear affected voices: Listen directly to persons with lived experience, families and mental health professionals, consistent with the bill’s own provisions on the composition of the National Suicide Prevention Task Force. The Senate has taken an important first step. The committee stage is where that commitment will be tested. Nigeria should choose protection over prosecution and enact a law that treats survivors of suicide attempts with the dignity, compassion and care to which they are entitled. •Angela Uwandu Uzoma-Iwuchukwu is Country Director, Avocats Sans Frontières France/Lawyers Without Borders). items.title: Pope will not need any therapy after cancer surgery – Doctors
items.description: Pope Leo XIV will not need therapy following an operation last week to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung, his doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican on Wednesday. Test results showed the 71-year-old’s cancer “was localised” and “a subsequent oncological assessment confirmed that no further therapy is required”, the statement said. Leo, who was only elected last year as the first US pope, told followers on October 11 that he would be having surgery to remove a nodule. The operation went ahead on October 13 at Rome’s Gemelli hospital. Doctors later revealed the growth was cancerous and they had to remove part of his right lung. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics left hospital on October 17 and on Sunday said he would resume his duties “gradually”. He said he wants to go ahead with a long-planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived for two decades, on November 6-17. items.title: Vladimir Putin, the Humanitarian
items.description: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.” — Steve Witkoff, U.S. special envoy to the Middle East, addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin Mark Wednesday, October 21, 2026, as “the day words lost all meaning.” My dictionary just ran outside and threw itself off a bridge. Noah Webster arose from his grave and lurched around, howling and tearing at his hair. Samuel Johnson is bellowing something awful; I can hear it across the Atlantic Ocean. George Orwell is sighing; he has been here before. I have to imagine that Putin is a little insulted at being so gravely misunderstood. With this single word, humanitarian , our envoy has revealed a stunning ignorance of the Russian president’s life’s work. This is like going to Picasso and praising him as a “representational painter,” or calling the Sahara “the wettest place in the world,” or describing Witkoff’s statement as “unembarrassing.” I see, perhaps, where the misunderstanding began. Putin referred to Trump as a “humanitarian,” and Witkoff thought to himself: Ah! This word clearly has a different meaning than I have been led to believe! I will have to reconstruct its definition from context clues . Maybe it’s someone with P in his name. Maybe it’s someone who doesn’t think that the United States should be in NATO. Maybe it’s someone who would look really good on horseback. Maybe no words mean anything! Maybe they are just phonemes to be thrown at a wall, at random, in the manner of that great representational painter Jackson Pollock. One of the conditions of freedom is that words have an understood meaning. If Putin is a humanitarian, then Dolly Parton was an axe murderer. Who else gets to be filed under humanitarian if Putin makes the cut? Stalin? The iceberg that sunk the Titanic? Calling Putin a humanitarian is like calling Hannibal Lecter a humanitarian, although there is more of a case to be made for Hannibal because he does, at least, subsist on people. Let me start over. It is nice and convenient, I think, when words have meaning. It makes it easier to order a sandwich. When words are more of a suggestion, reality evaporates at your touch, and none of your rights is secure. Good luck getting a sandwich then! Real is fake, fake is real, and all your society’s most precious values carry a disconcerting wink: freedom, free speech, meritocracy, equality. When you chant them, when you promise them to one another, you are not sure exactly what you are saying. Their meaning melts like hot wax, and homeland security becomes an unmarked car slamming into your neighbor. Authoritarians treat words as a game. (Putin, great humanitarian that he is, has some experience with this.) Perhaps war is peace (big news for the Nobel Committee, if true)! Perhaps the best humanitarian is whoever voids the world of the most people! Perhaps election integrity is the exact opposite of that! In the spirit of this new, callous disregard for words and their meaning, I say: Great job! Well done! What a magnificent time to be alive, when all of the best people are in charge.

items.title: Protests banned in parts of Paris as Macron swipes at Trump
items.description: Police banned protests in parts of Paris on Thursday, as France braced for more demonstrations just days after student and other rallies degenerated into some of the worst street unrest in years. Wednesday’s announcement came after President Emmanuel Macron took an apparent swipe at his US counterpart Donald Trump for exploiting the riots for political advantage in the US midterm election battle. The Paris ban will last from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm (0600 to 1800 GMT) and apply to key landmarks in the French capital, including the Elysee presidential palace, both houses of parliament, as well as tourist havens such as the Louvre museum and the Champs-Elysees. Other areas where rallies will be prohibited include the Bastille and Republique squares, and the Chatelet-Les Halles shopping area which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend. France has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings. As his government struggled to contain a crisis that has damaged France’s image abroad and rattled financial markets six months before presidential elections, Macron implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also fighting an election campaign, made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain. “There are people who campaign at France’s expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha. Trump has sought to link the unrest to “migrants, jihadists, and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging. He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies. Le Pen late Wednesday branded Macron’s remarks as “conspiratorial” in a post on X. “The images we saw last Saturday are not generated by artificial intelligence: they show the sad reality of what France has become after 10 years of Macronist rule,” added the far-right candidate, who is leading in the polls for the 2027 presidential election. Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France’s protests. – ‘New phase’ upcoming – The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France. Since the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of fresh cost-of-living demonstrations planned for Saturday, Macron’s government has warned it will brook no further violence. Fresh demonstrations planned by high school pupils and university students were similarly struck down in both Paris and the southeastern city of Lyon. Following a meeting on Wednesday with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the leader of France’s hardline CGT union, Sophie Binet, called for a “new phase” of protests, with strikes early next month. Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Wednesday that, of the 2,500 people taken into custody during and after the protests, 174 had been jailed. Another 917 had been formally prosecuted, he added. The convulsion in the EU’s second-biggest economy has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country’s growing debt pile and deficit. The yield on France’s benchmark 10-year bond passed five percent on Wednesday as investors demanded a higher return amid fiscal concerns. On Friday, the Moody’s ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France’s public debt. – ‘Quite disconcerting’ – France’s neighbours Italy and Belgium were also experiencing similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there. While the curfews imposed in several cities have helped calm the situation, they have disrupted some access to late-night public transport. “It’s quite disconcerting,” said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But “if it can prevent further acts of vandalism… then yes, I think it’s a good thing”, he said. The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend’s demonstrations announced Wednesday it plans a march on Saturday from Bastille square in Paris, and follow-up nationwide demonstrations on November 5. items.title: Arteta fears Saka injury after Arsenal’s Champions League draw with Bayern
items.description: Arsenal coach Mikel Arteta said the club was “concerned” about the severity of an injury to winger Bukayo Saka after Wednesday’s pulsating 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich. Saka, Arsenal’s joint top goalscorer this season alongside Victor Gyokeres, went off early after falling to the turf grabbing his thigh and was replaced by Eberechi Eze. Eze scored Arsenal’s opener and Declan Rice scored late to clinch a draw for last season’s runners up after an Alphonso Davies goal and a Harry Kane penalty for the hosts. Arteta said Saka’s injury was as yet unclear, but told reporters the club’s medical staff were worried. “They are a bit concerned about Saka. When a player has to come off with sharp pain it is never good news. We have to wait and see,” Arteta said. “The level of intensity this game requires as well is something incredible. You could see it last night, the PSG-Barcelona game. “The level that you need, it’s unbelievable. It’s the highest level and those things happen, unfortunately. “He doesn’t look good at all, but we’ll have to wait and see,” the Spaniard added. Arteta spoke glowingly of his side’s efforts, while praising those of the home side. “Bayern batter every team, so I really value what the boys did tonight,” he said. “That’s one of the highest levels we have played… The level of opposition and our level as well. It was two teams that wanted to attack and play.” Rice was thrilled with his late goal. “I’m so happy. When you play against teams like Bayern that are man-to-man all over the pitch, you have to apply certain principles,” Rice told TNT. “I just kept running, lost my marker and I was in on goal to score.” Vanguard News The post Arteta fears Saka injury after Arsenal’s Champions League draw with Bayern appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: L’association tunisienne ATun-DIPs récompensée au IPOPI BIG community award
items.description: L'Association tunisienne des patients atteints de déficits immunitaires primitifs ATun-DIPs a remporté le 3ᵉ prix du IPOPI BIG community award, une distinction internationale qui récompense les initiatives remarquables des associations de patients. Créée en 2018 dans le cadre du projet « Amélioration de la prise en charge des enfants Tunisiens atteints de Déficits Immunitaires Primitifs, ATun-DIP’s », porté par l’Institut Pasteur de Tunis et financé par la Direction de la Coopération Internationale de Monaco, l’association s’inscrit dans une dynamique visant à améliorer la prise en charge des patients atteints de déficits immunitaires primitifs (DIPs) en Tunisie. Cette distinction souligne l’engagement des membres d’ATUN-DIPs, présidée par Dr Meriam Ben Ali, chercheuse au laboratoire LTCII de l’Institut Pasteur de Tunis, en faveur de l’amélioration de la prise en charge des patients. Elle met en lumière la complémentarité entre recherche scientifique, expertise médicale et engagement associatif au service des patients et de leurs familles. À travers des initiatives menées en collaboration avec les professionnels de santé, les familles, les institutions nationales et les partenaires internationaux, ATUN-DIPs contribue à renforcer la sensibilisation aux DIPs, à favoriser le diagnostic précoce et à améliorer la qualité de vie des personnes concernées. L’Institut Pasteur de Tunis salue cette reconnaissance internationale, qui témoigne de l’importance de la collaboration entre recherche scientifique et associations de patients. items.title: ‘Real-world skill sets’ – Sam George makes case for One Million Coders programme
items.description: Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations Minister Sam Nartey George says the One Million Coders programme is designed to equip people with practical skills they can use in everyday life and business. Speaking at Joy News’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, he urged the public to enrol in the programme’s courses. His comments followed a question about scaling up training that helps ordinary people become more productive in their daily activities and businesses. George said that practical focus was central to the programme’s purpose. He described it as giving people “real-world skill sets that are applied in real-world situations.” He said about 37 programmes were currently running on the portal to help people acquire those skills. “It’s extremely important,” he said. His appeal emphasised how people apply their training. He explained that the programme aims to give participants skills useful in the situations they encounter. The minister also raised concerns about data sovereignty when businesses use foreign technology platforms. He questioned whether contractual assurances sufficiently protect data held by those providers. “That is a mirage that is sold to many African companies, not just Ghanaian companies.” George cited the U.S. Cloud Act as the basis for his concerns. He argued that it superseded private agreements promising data protection and sovereignty. He said he had discussed those concerns with Google and Amazon Web Services. The minister urged greater scrutiny of agreements with foreign providers, particularly where health records were involved.

items.title: Sénatoriales en Guinée : la DGE fixe une exigence incontournable aux candidats
items.description: À moins de deux mois des élections sénatoriales prévues le 20 décembre 2026, la Direction générale des élections (DGE) précise les conditions de recevabilité des dossiers de candidature. Dans un communiqué daté du 21 octobre, l’institution rappelle que chaque candidat doit obligatoirement présenter un suppléant, dont le dossier devra comporter les mêmes pièces justificatives que celui du titulaire. « Pour être recevable, chaque dossier de candidature doit obligatoirement être accompagné des pièces d’un candidat suppléant » , souligne la DGE dans son communiqué. L’institution précise également que le suppléant doit fournir exactement les mêmes documents que le candidat titulaire. La DGE invite ainsi les candidats à veiller à la complétude de leurs dossiers et au respect des délais de dépôt. « La DGE invite par conséquent l’ensemble des candidats à veiller à la présentation de tous les documents requis pour le titulaire et son suppléant ainsi qu’au respect strict du délai de dépôt des dossiers de candidature » , indique le communiqué. Pour toute information complémentaire, les candidats sont invités à se rapprocher des démembrements de la Direction générale des élections.

items.title: A case for a systematic rollout of Ghana’s new traffic law (L.I. 2519
items.description: The Government of Ghana recently announced the rollout of a new set of road traffic regulations, aiming to curb the spate of road accidents in the country. Like any other efforts by previous administrations which sought to deal with the carnage on our roads, the new regulations could, by intent, be a positive move. The law must, however be rolled out systematically and implemented thoughtfully, else it is bound to fail. The regulations in question, ‘Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519)’, stand to fail if the government enforces all penalties simultaneously. The law, as has been put out, covers dozens of offences, from speeding to preaching in moving vehicles, with penalties that have jumped dramatically from what pertained in the old regulations. Three structural barriers make a “big bang” approach unworkable: Drivers are largely uninformed about the new rules, enforcement infrastructure is not ready, and compliance costs are stacking up. The government must adopt a phased, systematic rollou t that prioritizes fatal offences, builds infrastructure first, and educates the general public, and those the new rules affect directly in particular, before it penalizes offenders. Changes in the new L.I from the old law appear drastic. This amounts to a sweeping overhaul. The law covers offences ranging from street racing, jumping red lights, and failing to stop at STOP signs to parking in disabled designated spaces and unauthorised use of bus stops. Preaching or hawking in a moving commercial vehicle now also carries a jail term of three to eight months, up from the previous maximum of 30 days, while fines range from 5 penalty units to 200 penalty units, with one penalty unit valued at GH¢12 . What makes a law like this problematic is that, when you put these many behaviours together and criminalise them at once, you create a situation where a large portion of drivers are technically in violation of something. That undermines the moral authority of the law and makes selective enforcement inevitable. One key concern regarding the coming of this new road traffic law is that there has not been adequate public and stakeholder engagement. The Ghana Private Road Transport Union (GPRTU) has stated that its members were not consulted before the L.I was passed, and remain unaware of the new rules. How can drivers comply with a law they do not understand? The Ministry of Transport launched a nationwide education exercise in September 2026, with Transport Minister Joseph Bukari Nikpe acknowledging that nationwide education was “necessary to help drivers, transport operators, motor unions and other road users understand their responsibilities”. But one month of sensitization is certainly not enough time to absorb dozens of new offences and changed penalties. As the GPRTU has argued, drivers need to be properly educated before enforcement begins. Penalizing people for violations they did not know existed is not enforcement—it is ambush. It is a fact and legitimate argument to make also that the government has not put in place the needed infrastructure that will cater for effective implementation of the new law. CUTS International, a policy think tank, has publicly called on the government to delay full enforcement until traffic lights and road markings at enforcement locations have been inspected and repaired. Their concerns are specific: some traffic lights across Accra are obscured by overgrown trees, others are damaged or out of service. At some junctions, one of two traffic lights works while the other does not. Faded lane markings and stop lines make it impossible for drivers to know where they should stop. CUTS further put it bluntly: “The purpose of TRAFFITECH-GH is safer roads, not tickets arising from traffic lights drivers could not see” And, it is worth noting that the government itself has acknowledged the need for more preparation. The Ghana Police Service rescheduled the full implementation of TRAFFITECH-GH from October 1 to November 1, specifically to allow for “more extensive public awareness and education.” This postponement is tacit recognition that the original timeline was too aggressive. The compliance cost of new driver’s licence presents yet another element of challenge. The GPRTU has warned that the new licensing requirements could leave commercial drivers paying for up to three different licences—a professional driver’s licence, a separate commercial driver’s licence, and existing MMDA permits. The union’s deputy PRO pointed out: “It will not help businesses because if it happens like that, then it means we will be paying too much, increasing our operational cost”. The mandatory towing requirement adds another layer of cost. Vehicle owners must now subscribe to a towing service or hold an insurance policy with towing cover. The previous 30-minute to one-hour grace period has been eliminated entirely—vehicles must be towed immediately upon breakdown. After 21 days, vehicles can be auctioned. The GPRTU opposes the auction provision, arguing that “nobody will intentionally leave his vehicle on the road”, and that owners should be allowed to reclaim vehicles after paying towing and storage fees. What happens in this circumstance is that when compliance costs rise sharply while enforcement expands simultaneously, drivers face a rational calculation: the cost of obeying may exceed the cost of violating. That is not a recipe for compliance. Statistically, the data on Ghana’s road accident deaths suggests the need for prioritization. Ghana recorded 2,949 road deaths in 2025, the highest in 35 years and an 18.2% increase over 2024. Speeding accounted for more than 60% of all collision s . Motorcycle crashes rose by 19.4%, with 6,548 motorcycles involved in crashes. If the government focuses enforcement resources on these killers—speeding, drunk driving, red-light running, motorcycle helmet use—the safety gains will be immediate and measurable. Spreading limited enforcement capacity across preaching, hawking, parking violations, and administrative offences dilutes the impact on what actually kills people. The police have already indicated that the initial phase of TRAFFITECH-GH will focus on speeding. This is the right instinct. It should be formalized into policy. To ensure effective implementation of the new road traffic regulations, enforce should focus strictly on offences with the clearest link to fatalities: speeding, red-light running, drunk driving, motorcycle helmet use, and seat belt use. These have the strongest public consensus and the highest safety return. An equally important measure is to include offences that require physical infrastructure to comply with, such as stopping at YIELD signs, pedestrian crossing rules, bus stop regulations. Here, the relevant infrastructure should be provided before enforcement. Where such infrastructure exists, it should be functional. The introduction of administrative and nuisance offences should come last. By that point drivers would have experienced a functioning system for about a year and understand the expectations. It is expected for some to argue that gradualism signals weakness—that the government is not serious, that indiscipline continues while authorities tiptoe. The 2,949 deaths demand urgency. But urgency does not require chaos. The government can signal seriousness by strictly enforcing a focused set of critical offences while phasing in the rest. Here the message becomes: “We are serious about saving lives, and we are doing this properly.” That is more credible than a blitz that collapses under its own weight, breeds corruption, and alienates the very drivers whose cooperation is essential. In all, L.I. 2519 contains the right intentions. But good intentions do not make good policy. A law that overwhelms the enforcement system, punishes drivers for infrastructure failures, and imposes costs that make compliance irrational will not save lives. It will generate resentment, bribery, and evasion. A systematic, phased approach—prioritizing fatal offences, building infrastructure first, and educating before penalizing—gives the law a chance to work. The goal is not to punish the maximum number of people. The goal is to reduce the 2,949 deaths. That requires strategy, not shock therapy. Before issuing any fine, there should be complete visibility inspections at every enforcement location. Repair obscured signals, repaint faded markings, install missing speed limit signs. There should be face-to-face education with commercial driver unions. Equally, there should be verification to ensure that the vehicles registration database can accurately identify offenders.

items.title: Sam George outlines $270m Ghana AI investment, cites risks of feeding government data into foreign models
items.description: The Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, has outlined a $270 million investment in Ghana’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, with $250 million earmarked for infrastructure and computing capacity and the remaining $20 million for seed funding for an AI fund. He said the investment would support the development of Ghana’s AI infrastructure, including a national language-processing model, amid concerns about sensitive government information being fed into foreign AI platforms. Speaking during JoyNews’ Digital Economy Forum on AI and the Ghana Economy on Wednesday, October 21, Mr George said he had observed instances where classified government material was being entered into platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude by analysts working in ministers’ offices. “That for me represents a critical national risk because memos, government material, critical government sensitive data is being fed into these systems by analysts sitting in ministers’ offices to process that data,” he said. He questioned the effectiveness of the country’s data residency law if government institutions continued to rely on foreign AI models to process sensitive information. “Now we have a residency law that we’ve passed, but it’s useless if the government system itself is using a foreign AI model to do processing,” he said. Mr George said the government was working towards developing what he called the “Ghana Chat”, a national language-processing model that would allow government institutions to use AI while building local capacity. He said the initiative was also intended to ensure that the public sector benefited from the speed and computing power of AI without compromising sensitive government data. The Minister acknowledged that the proposed model would not initially match the capabilities of established platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude but said its performance would improve through continued use and training. “At start, will it be as effective as Claude and ChatGPT? Definitely not. But then the more you use it and the more you teach it, the more the machines learn, the better the system will get,” he said. He added that existing AI systems had been built, piloted and trained using billions, if not trillions, of data points, suggesting that Ghana’s model would similarly require time and training to improve. Mr George acknowledged the questions and concerns raised about the initiative but expressed confidence that the proposed approach would help address the issues. “So basically I see all the questions that are being raised, very legitimate questions, very legitimate issues, but I believe that we are on the right track to resolving all of those issues,” he said.

items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI, a adressé un message de félicitations aux membres de l'équipe nationale de futsal qui a remporté, mercredi soir à Rabat, la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations de futsal (Maroc-2026). Dans ce message, le Roi exprime aux membres de l'équipe nationale de futsal Ses chaleureuses félicitations et Sa grande fierté après avoir remporté la huitième édition de la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations de futsal que la capitale du Royaume a brillamment abritée, avec l'hospitalité traditionnelle reconnue du Maroc. Le Souverain exprime Ses félicitations aux membres de l'équipe nationale, et à travers eux à l'ensemble des cadres techniques et administratifs de la Fédération Royale Marocaine de Football, pour cet exploit renouvelé, fruit de « votre performance professionnelle remarquable et de haute qualité, de la détermination inébranlable à conserver le titre pour le Maroc pour la quatrième fois consécutive, et du patriotisme sincère en vue de confirmer et de consolider la place de Notre pays parmi les grandes sélections, tant sur le plan continental qu’international ». Saluant de nouveau l'exceptionnelle prestation des membres de l'équipe nationale qui « ont hissé, une fois encore, bien haut l'étendard de Notre chère Patrie lors de cette grand-messe africaine », le Roi implore le Tout-Puissant de leur accorder davantage de succès pour remporter de nouveaux titres et réaliser de nouvelles performances lors des prochaines échéances, tout en les assurant de Sa Haute sollicitude et bienveillance.
